Margaret of Hungary, daughter of King Bela I, spent her whole life as a Dominican nun. Her parents had vowed their next child to religion when Hungary was freed from the Tatars. Born in 1242, she entered the Veszprem convent in 1245. She took the habit at four. At ten she moved to her parents' convent on Margaret Island near Buda.

She refused her father's plan for a marriage to Ottokar II of Bohemia. She took solemn vows at eighteen. She lived in contemplation, fasting, and hard penance, including a hair garment and an iron girdle. Venerated at once after her death in 1271, she was never canonized. Pius VI allowed her veneration in 1789, and her feast falls on 18 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breviary:
The Breviary, the book holding the whole canonical office, began as an abridgment and grew into a full liturgical library in one volume. Its name first meant a book of rubrics, a sort of Ordo, and the title for a book with the entire office dates from the eleventh century. Gregory VII's abridged Roman Court order gave the name fresh force, since breviary means abridgment.

Six parts organize the entry: definition, contents, the hours, component parts of the office, history, and reforms. It traces early uses by Alcuin and Prudentius of Troyes, the Monte Cassino Ordo of about 1100, and the growth from scattered books, Psalter, Antiphonary, Responsoriary, and Lectionary, into one work. The name itself is illogical today, since such a book should be a Plenarium, not an abridgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breviary-hymn:
The Breviary Hymns of the Rosary, four hymns for the feast's proper office granted by Leo XIII on 5 August 1888, compress each mystery into a single stanza. Some critics credited Leo himself, famed for his Latin verse and Rosary devotion, but the hymns trace to the Dominican Office of 1834 and to Eustace Sirena, a devout client of Mary. They later reached Segovia in 1841 and Venice in 1848.

Each hymn holds five four-line stanzas of classical dimeter iambics, apart from the shared doxology. First Vespers sings the Joyful Mysteries, Matins the Sorrowful, and Lauds the Glorious, one stanza per mystery. Second Vespers sums all three sets in three stanzas. A frame stanza gathers them whole, and a closing call bids the singer weave from the rosary a flower crown for the Mother of fair love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bribery:
Bribery, the payment or promise of money to bend a public trust to private gain, is judged here on moral grounds alone. Judges must serve justice without fear or favor, and those who appoint officers, award contracts, enforce laws, or elect lawmakers must seek the common good. Taking a bribe for such acts betrays the trust and shares guilt for the unfit or crooked men put in place.

Hard cases test the rule, since a voter may see little difference between candidates and feel no injustice in selling his vote. The entry still calls the act immoral and rightly banned by law. A bribe blinds judgment, blunts discrimination, and leaves the voter unable to weigh whether his man is worthy of the post he seeks to fill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caius-3rd-cen:
Caius, also called Kay or Key, was a physician and scholar born at Norwich on 6 October 1510 who died at London on 29 July 1573. He entered Cambridge in 1529, took his M.A. in 1535, and studied medicine at Padua under Montanus and Vesalius, earning his doctorate there in 1541. After touring Italy, France, and Germany he returned to England in 1544 and lectured on anatomy in London for twenty years.

His book on the sweating sickness of 1552 stands as the best account of that epidemic, and he also translated and commented on Galen and Hippocrates. With his medical earnings he refounded his Cambridge college, Gonville, in 1558, ever since known as Gonville and Caius College. He served as royal physician under Edward VI and Elizabeth until dismissed in 1568 for his Catholic faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-ere:
A religious house is a fixed home for religious persons, a community in the strict sense, ruled by a superior and keeping its order's rule. It differs from a grange or farm, a villa for recreation, and a hospice for traveling religious. Lawful erection needs the Holy See's permission, certain in countries under the decree Romanos Pontifices, including the United States and England, and required also for Italy.

It also needs the assent of the ordinary, a rule approved at Chalcedon in 451 and restored by Trent after mendicant privileges had worn it down. The bishop must hear those the house might harm, such as nearby orders or the local people, though the parish priest cannot object unless parochial rights are granted. Twelve religious must be provided for, or the house falls under the ordinary. Moving a house within one place needs no Roman permission, since that is transfer, not erection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canterbury:
Canterbury served as England's leading archbishopric from 597 until 1558, when Cardinal Pole, the last Catholic archbishop, died. The entry opens with Augustine's mission from Gregory the Great. It tells of his welcome from Queen Bertha of Kent. It recounts the conversion of King Ethelbert with many thousands of Saxons in the year of Augustine's landing.

Gregory had planned archbishoprics at London and York, yet Augustine's success fixed the southern see at Canterbury instead. Later sections trace the archbishops, metropolitan rights, the diocese, the cathedral, and the see's history. Drawing on Bede and a long shelf of local histories, the entry covers a church that shaped English Christianity for nearly a thousand years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-category:
Category began as a Greek legal word for accusation, which Aristotle turned into a logical term for attributing a predicate to a subject. Boethius gave it the Latin name predicament. The categories are the widest classes of predicates that can be said of an individual thing, the highest genera under which narrower ideas fall.

Whether Aristotle meant them as divisions of words, ideas, or things is still debated, and the article shows how they fit each reading. Taken as ideas they belong to logic, as words to grammar, and as things to ontology, where they name the ultimate classes of finite being. The piece defends the scheme as a workable simplification of reality for inquiry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chambery:
Chambéry is an archdiocese covering the whole arrondissement of Chambéry in Savoy, except eight communes, plus communes around Annecy and Albertville. In 1467 Paul II set up a chapter answering directly to the Holy See. It met in the ducal chapel that Amadeus IX of Savoy and Yolande of France had built for the Holy Winding-Sheet. Sixtus IV joined it to the deanery of Savoy.

Leo X made the deanery an archbishopric in 1515, but Francis I objected. Only in 1775 did Pius VI separate it from Grenoble, creating it a bishopric with its see at Chambéry in 1779. Revolutionary France formed the constitutional Diocese of Mont-Blanc in 1792. The 1802 Concordat set up a Chambéry-Geneva diocese, and a bull of 1817 made Chambéry an archdiocese with Aosta as suffragan. At the close of 1905 it counted 164,424 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-changanacherr:
Changanacherry is a Vicariate Apostolic in Travancore, British India, created on 28 July 1896. Its first vicar apostolic in fact, Mathew Makil, Bishop of Tralles in title, was consecrated on 25 October 1896. The vicariate was founded to serve the Syro-Malabar Rite's Native Indian Christians. Five deaneries of Nordist Syrians, descended from native Malabar castes, and two of Sudists, descended from fourth-century immigrant Syrians, belong to it.

Its territory runs south to Purakad, bounded north by the Vicariate of Ernakulam, east by the Ghats, and west by the Gulf of Arabia. Catholics number 140,172 out of 900,000 people, served by 95 churches and 57 chapels and a native clergy of 283. Schools flourish: 418 native parish schools hold 14,328 pupils, and a Malayalam weekly paper speaks for the Catholic press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chantry:
A chantry endows priests to sing or say Mass for its founder's soul, or for souls named by him. Most also performed other offices: singing in a collegiate church or cathedral choir, curate in outlying districts, chaplain in hospitals and jails, or schoolmaster or librarian. The institution was essentially liturgical, and it needed a place where the incumbent could say Mass.

As a rule, space was screened off between the great pillars of a nave or transept and an altar erected there. Sometimes an addition opening into the choir was built, or a detached building. Detached chantry chapels, in churchyards, outlying districts, or at bridge entrances, often had two stories: the lower for religious uses and the upper as the incumbent's home or schoolroom. Founding a chantry needed the ordinary's consent and a fund large enough for its building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chartulary:
An entry on the chartulary, a medieval book or roll holding copies of documents about the foundation, privileges, and legal rights of churches, towns, guilds, schools, and families. Also called a cartularium or codex diplomaticus, it sometimes means a bound set of originals rather than copies. Gregory of Tours mentions rolls of charters in the sixth century. The oldest surviving chartularies date from the tenth, and those from the tenth to the thirteenth centuries are very numerous.

Copyists sometimes reproduced originals exactly and sometimes altered wording, modernised names, or even changed the sense to stretch a privilege. A chartulary's worth as history therefore turns on how faithfully it keeps the original meaning, a question for historical criticism. The entry ranks an honest chartulary above a private letter or a chronicler's tale, and points to the great French catalogues and to Gross on English sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-children-of-m:
An entry on the Sodality of the Children of Mary Immaculate, a confraternity for young girls that grew from the apparition of the Miraculous Medal. The Virgin appeared to Sister Catherine Labouré, a Paris novice of the Daughters of Charity, in 1830, and trial associations soon formed in houses of the order. A rescript of June 1847 empowered the superior general to erect the confraternity in every Sisters of Charity house for girls in their schools and workrooms.

The same favour was extended in 1850 to boys taught by the Lazarist priests and the Sisters of Charity, and in 1876 Pius the Ninth opened membership to girls outside those schools. Leo the Thirteenth confirmed the privileges in 1897 and 1903. Members wear the Miraculous Medal on a blue ribbon, and by 1897 the sodality counted 100,000 living members worldwide, with 400,000 registered since its first canonical erection at Paris in 1847.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chivalry:
An entry on chivalry, the institution of the medieval knight, viewed from its military, social, and religious sides and traced to its fall. In war, chivalry meant the heavy cavalry that formed the chief force of the age. Its marks were costly arms, from the mail coat of the Crusades to the plate armour of the fourteenth century. A knight needed at least three horses, for battle, travel, and baggage, plus attendants to bear the shield and help him mount.

Socially, chivalry softened into courtly display, with jousts, tournaments, and banquet-hall vows. The Vow of the Swan dates to 1306, and the Vow of the Pheasant to 1454, when 150 knights swore to rescue Constantinople and achieved nothing. Literature first lifted chivalry, then mocked it, from Chaucer to Cervantes. Revived infantry, Swiss pikemen, and at last gunpowder ended the horseman's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrismal-chri:
An entry on the chrismal and chrismatory, the vessels that hold the holy oils consecrated by the bishop on Holy Thursday. Those oils are oil of catechumens, oil of the sick, and chrism, which gives the vessels their name. The word chrismal once meant other things too. It named a cloth sheath for relics, a pall or corporal, and a vessel for the Eucharist. It also named the long white hooded robes of the newly baptised, worn from Holy Saturday to Low Sunday.

In present use the two words mean the oil vessels. One set keeps the yearly supply in the cathedral sacristy, the other holds the daily need in the parish church. Both must be gold, silver, tin, or pewter. Longer vessels look like little jars, smaller ones like jointed cylindrical boxes. Each bears a stamped letter for its oil, so the oils are never confused.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-histor:
A vast entry on church history, the scientific study and methodical telling of the Church's growth in time. History in general traces how human life changes through facts, events, and situations, and religion's history among peoples is its noblest form. Reason holds there is one true religion, and revelation shows it to be the Christian religion, in particular the Catholic Church, visible and concrete.

Church history therefore studies the institution Jesus Christ founded and the Holy Spirit guides for human salvation. Religion is social by nature, since moral life binds people together, and Christianity all the more aims at organisation. The entry sets out the nature, office, sources, and divisions of the discipline, from its method to its periods. It defends its place as the most important and edifying branch of the history of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerestory:
A clerestory once meant any traceried opening or window in a church, in an aisle, tower, cloister, or screen. Now it means the windows in an aisled nave, or the wall holding the high windows. Sometimes these windows are very small, mere quatrefoils or spherical triangles. Yet in large buildings they matter greatly for beauty and utility, above all where nave and side aisles allow light to enter from above the aisle roofs into the church body.

Fergusson's theory holds that Greek temple interiors were lit by a clerestory, similar inside to those of great Egyptian temples but adapted outside to a sloping roof. Countersinking into the roof made three ridges where light entered, while the roof's regular shape and ridge lines stayed intact between openings. All surviving remains and ancient descriptions support the theory, the article says, though Simpson regards it as extremely improbable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraternity:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats the Confraternity of the Holy Rosary, following his Rosary article's verdict: no sound evidence places any Rosary confraternity before the last quarter of the fifteenth century. Dominican guilds existed, but proof linking them to the Rosary fails. Through Alan de Rupe's preaching, associations rose shortly before 1475. Cologne's 1474 foundation by Father James Sprenger stands most famous, drawing enrollees worldwide. A 1486 Plumpton letter shows a London priest registering his Yorkshire patron's name with Our Lady of Cologne.

Later forms widen the picture. The Perpetual Rosary organizes day-and-night recitation among associates taking allotted shares. The Living Rosary, begun in 1826 and independent of the confraternity, rings fifteen members who each say one decade daily, completing the whole Rosary together. Another Rosary confraternity dates from the seventeenth century. Thurston thus guards the early history against assumption, while mapping the living devotions that grew from it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Francesca Steele's entry follows the Congregation of Our Lady of Calvary, founded at Poitiers in 1617 by Antoinette of Orléans-Longueville with Capuchin Father Joseph Le Clerc du Tremblay. Widowed in 1596, Antoinette entered Toulouse's Feuillantines in 1599. After profession the pope made her coadjutrix to Fontevrault's abbess for reform work. There she met Father Joseph, her director, fresh from l'Encloître's reform. When Paul V ordered a training seminary, that convent filled with novices. In 1614 Antoinette built a new Poitiers convent to Our Lady of Calvary, cradle of the congregation.

With papal leave she left Fontevrault, taking nuns who sought the strict Benedictine rule. Fontevrault's abbess first consented, then objected. Only after Antoinette's death did Father Joseph set constitutions and win Gregory XV's erecting bull. The Holy See finally approved it on 17 January 1827. Revolution crushed it, restoration revived it, and by 1860 twenty French houses stood, seven surviving.

Sister Mary St. David's entry follows the Presentation of Mary congregation, devoted to educating young girls. Mother Marie Rivier founded it in 1796 at Theuyts, Ardèche. The mother-house stands at Saint-Andéol, Ardèche, under superior general Mother Marie Ste-Honorine. Canada's provincial house, founded 18 October 1853 by Mgr Prince, first Bishop of Saint Hyacinthe, doubles as mother-house, where vows are made.

First six, led by Mother Marie St-Maurice, settled at Sainte-Marie de Monnoir, where pastor Crevier had prepared a convent. They opened a boarding school and a day class, both prosperous. The novitiate moved to Saint Hugues in 1855, then to Saint Hyacinthe in 1858, into a convent lately held by Montreal's Notre Dames. Cramped quarters forced a large new building near the seminary, occupied 1876, the older house an academy. An annex followed, students installed in 1907. Thirty Canadian houses and sixteen American houses educate 13,670 children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
Florence McGahan's entry covers two Mount Calvary congregations, first the Daughters. Virginia Centurione, Genoa's Doge's daughter and Gasparo Grimaldi Bracelli's wife, founded them in 1619. In famine she gathered abandoned children into Monte Calvario's Santa Maria del Refugio dei Tribolati. Associates chose common life, Francis's rule, and service of poor and sick, bound by a solemn promise of perseverance, not vows. Marquess Brignole funded a second house in 1641, earning sisters the Brignole name.

Pius VII invited them to Rome in 1815, and Gregory XVI assigned an Esquiline house near Saint Norbert's in 1833. Hubert Charpentier formed the Missionary Society in 1633, priests honoring the Sacred Passion and spreading the Faith in Huguenot regions. First houses stood at Betharram and Notre Dame de Ceraison. Joined with a Capuchin association on Mont-Valérien at Louis XIII's instance, it won royal confirmation in 1650. Paris pastors joined, pilgrimages flowed there, but Revolution ended it.

The entry surveys Heart of Mary congregations, beginning with Nancy's Sisters. Mgr Menjaud, Bishop of Nancy and Toul, founded them in 1842 to teach girls trades and protect their virtue. Masson's statutes let them own only their houses, sending surplus to poor children and altar decoration. Perpetual Adoration graced the mother-house. Delaplace and Marie-Jeanne Moisan founded Paris's Sister-servants in 1860, teaching children and visiting the sick at hospitals and homes. Canada flourished with about 140 sisters and 2,500 children, plus six American communities.

Kobès founded Dakar's Daughters on 24 May 1858 for native women in Senegambia. Dupuis founded Pondicherry's Congregation at the synod's desire for young Indian girls' education. Pico Heights, Los Angeles, gained Sisters in July 1848. Rennes ladies running an incurables' home took the Daughters name in 1841. Turgeon and Marie Roy founded Quebec's Sister-Servants in 1859, with Monroe, Michigan, holding a sister foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-arch:
A biographical entry follows Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury, who died on 25 October 758. First heard of as Abbot of Liminge in Kent, he became Bishop of Hereford in 736. He was moved to Canterbury around 740. Journeying to Rome, he received the pallium, the woollen band marking an archbishop, and attended the Council of Clovesho in 742.

At his second Council of Clovesho in 747, called at Pope Zachary's wish, many canons guided monks' lives and bishops' and priests' duties. The council insisted that catechetical teaching be given in English. Its proceedings, sent to Saint Boniface, prompted similar reform in Germany. Cuthbert also won a great change for Canterbury. Archbishops, once buried at Saints Peter and Paul, were henceforth interred at Christ Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-nicolas:
A life of Denis-Nicolas Le Nourry, a Maurist Benedictine writer born at Dieppe in 1647 who died at Saint-Germain in Paris in 1724. Schooled by Oratorians at home, he entered the Benedictines at Jumièges in 1665 and later helped publish Cassiodorus at Rouen and Ambrose at Rouen and Paris. His last forty years were spent in Paris.

His chief work, the Apparatus, appeared in two volumes in 1703 and 1715 as a guide to the Lyons collection of the Fathers. Long dissertations give each writer's life, the aim and genuineness of each work, and the age that shaped it. A 1710 edition argues that a tract on persecutors came from Lucius Caecilius rather than Lactantius, and he also edited Lactantius, Hilarianus, and a fragment on human origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devotion-to-t:
A historical survey of devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary, read as the Communion of Saints put into practice. Early centuries show no clear trace of Marian cult. The first plain saintly honour goes to martyrs, whose tombs hosted the sacrifice and whose yearly birthdays Christians kept from the second century. Tertullian and Cyprian sharpened the sense that martyrs win graces for others, and direct invocation followed.

Later ages widen the picture. The Collyridians' cake offerings drew Epiphanius's rebuke. Merovingian and Carolingian times fixed feasts such as the Assumption, and after 1000 devotion took organized shape in countless practices. Modern pages highlight the Litany of Loreto, the Lourdes apparitions of 1858, and the miraculous medal of Notre-Dame des Victoires in Paris.

A doctrinal and historical entry on devotion to the Heart of Mary, twin to the Sacred Heart devotion yet distinct from it. True devotion needs two things together. Homage must aim at the physical heart itself. Reading in it means seeing her inner life: joys and sorrows, virtues, and above all her love for God, for her divine Son, and for sinful children. Either element alone falls short.

History links the devotion with that of the Heart of Jesus while keeping its own thread, which the Gospel invites with quiet delicacy. Feast days vary by place: the Sunday after the Assumption octave, the third Sunday after Pentecost, early July, the Eudist feast of 8 February, and Notre-Dame-des-Victoires before Lent. No feast has yet been granted to the whole Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocesan-chan:
The diocesan chancery is the office that handles all written papers used in governing a diocese. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places it under the bishop or his deputy, where documents are drawn up, copied, sent on, and filed. A record is kept of every official writing that goes out or comes in. The officer in charge is called the diocesan chancellor.

In many dioceses the chancellor holds powers that elsewhere belong only to the vicar-general. This is commonest in small dioceses run directly by the bishop, where the vicar-general is called only when the bishop is away or hindered. The entry thus opens a window onto the quiet paperwork that keeps a diocese running.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Members of cathedral or collegiate chapters who hold both a foremost place and a measure of jurisdiction are ecclesiastical dignitaries. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the usual dignities as provost and dean, with custos and scholasticus at times. Their nomination and canonical institution rest largely with the pope, under common church law, special legislation such as concordats, and custom.

Dignities differ from personates, whose holders hold only a fixed right of precedence. They differ again from offices such as canon theologian or canon penitentiary, which imply only a charge or duty. The entry cites Wernz, Laurentius, and Sagmuller, giving readers the ranks within a chapter in short compass.

Ecclesiastical heraldry splits into several branches, chiefly the arms of religious bodies and the insignia of church rank and office. It also covers the charges and forms of general heraldry with a religious origin or use. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds the emblems of saints and other beings honored by the Church. Through all these runs symbolism, real, suggested, or fancied, and close woven with rank insignia lies the lore of vestments.

The origin of heraldry itself stays shrouded in mystery, a growth from three ideas, none of which alone can explain it. The entry works through corporations, dignities, and saints' devices, citing Woodward, Fox-Davies, and Battandier. For readers of shields and seals, it is a full guide to the Church's pictured language.

An ecclesiastical seminary is a school set up under a decree of the Council of Trent to train the diocesan clergy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry warns that the bare word seminary means other things, a university circle in Germany or a young ladies' academy in England and America. Qualified by ecclesiastical, it names only the diocesan school, distinct from the novitiate and scholasticate of religious orders.

In the seminary, spiritual and intellectual formation go together, unlike a university faculty of theology, which is not a seminary. The entry surveys seminaries across the English-speaking world, with acts of the Holy See, histories of houses, and essays on training. It points readers to the American colleges at Louvain and Rome among special articles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-embroidery:
Church embroidery is the subject of this entry, which traces needlework on vestments from early times to its high point. For the period before the tenth century no full account survives, and no church embroidery of that age is preserved. The oldest pieces known are a maniple and stole from the early tenth century at Durham, and fragments of an altar cover of the same age at Ravenna.

Magnificent work appears in the eleventh century, such as a chasuble wholly covered with pictures in pure gold at Bamberg, and the coronation mantle of Hungary, once also a chasuble. Gold thread ruled church work until the thirteenth century, though silk was also used, as splendid copes at Saint Paul in Carinthia show. Embroidery reached its fullest flower in the thirteenth, fourteenth, and early fifteenth centuries, using gold, silver, and silk, with stamped disks and enamel spangles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-espousals-of-:
The Espousals of the Blessed Virgin Mary is a feast of the Latin Church. Joseph and Mary certainly contracted a real matrimony. Still Mary is called espoused to Joseph, because the marriage was never consummated. Peter d'Ailly and his disciple Gerson were the first energetic propagators of devotion to Saint Joseph.

Gerson worked many years for a special votive feast of the virginal espousal of Mary and Joseph. His friend Henry Chicoti, canon of Chartres, left money for celebrating this feast in the cathedral, for which Gerson composed an Office. The first definite feast dates from 29 August 1517, when Leo X granted it to the Nuns of the Annunciation. This feast was celebrated on 22 October as a double of the second class. Its Mass honoured the Virgin exclusively and hardly mentioned Joseph, so it did not match Gerson's idea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethical-aspec:
In Greek and Roman civilization slavery formed an essential element of the social structure, and ethical speculators and statesmen alike regarded it as just and indispensable. The Greek assumed slaves should normally come only from barbarian or lower races. Roman law in the empire's heyday treated the slave as a mere chattel. The master held power of life and death over him; the slave could make no contract and had no civil rights; in law he was not a person.

Nevertheless natural justice condemned, or at least disapproved, masters who treated slaves with signal inhumanity. Christianity found slavery throughout the Roman world, and in power did not attempt summarily to abolish it. From the beginning, however, the Church pressed steadily for ameliorating the individual slave's condition. It pressed ultimately for abolishing a system hardly reconcilable with the Gospel and the brotherhood of all men in Divine sonship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eudists-socie:
The Eudists, or Society of Jesus and Mary, were instituted at Caen, France, on 25 March 1643, by Jean Eudes. The society's works are the education of priests in seminaries and the giving of missions. The end he assigned to his society made him decide against religious vows. He believed priests, finding in their dignity the means of rising to perfection, could inspire clerics with an idea of the priesthood.

He felt bishops would less willingly give seminaries to priests not subject to them. Father Eudes shared the opinions of Cardinal de Bérulle and Father Olier, who opposed religious vows in the orders they founded. Even Saint Vincent de Paul admitted vows only after hesitation, and on condition that his Priests of the Mission form an ecclesiastical society, not a religious order. The Society is therefore not a religious order, but an ecclesiastical body under the bishops, forming the clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-o-curr:
Eugene O'Curry was an Irish scholar, born at Dunaha near Carrigaholt, County Clare, in 1796 and dead in 1862. His father, a modest farmer, was an Irish scholar and a fine singer, steeped in his people's traditions. Eugene grew up amid Irish surroundings and soon learned to read the Irish manuscripts still common among the people. After the fall of Napoleon in 1815, agricultural distress in Ireland broke up the O'Curry farm.

In 1834 Eugene joined the men engaged upon the topographical and historical part of the Ordnance Survey of Ireland, with Petrie, Wakeman, Clarence Mangan the poet, and John O'Donovan. Seeking information on Irish places, he visited the British Museum, the Bodleian, Trinity College Library, the Royal Irish Academy, and other places. But the Government, afraid of the national memories the work evoked, abandoned the survey a few years later and dissolved the staff.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Holy Name of Mary feast honours Mary and all the graces given through her. It began at Cuenca in Spain in 1513, on the octave day of Mary's Nativity, 15 September. Sixtus V later moved it to 17 September after the Breviary reform. Spain and Naples received it in 1671 under its original title.

After Sobieski's victory at Vienna in 1683, Innocent XI spread it to the whole Church. The feast fell on the Sunday after Mary's Nativity each year. If a higher feast displaced it, the day moved to 12 September. Piarists and Marianists keep it as their own patronal feast today.

The Holy Rosary feast falls on the first Sunday of October each year. It grew from thanksgiving for the great naval victory at Lepanto in 1571. Pius V ordered a commemoration of the Rosary on that day. Gregory XIII let churches with a Rosary altar keep the feast.

Clement X extended the feast to all of Spain in 1671. After Prince Eugene's victory in 1716, Clement XI spread it to the universal Church. Leo XIII raised its rank and added Queen of the Most Holy Rosary. On the feast, Rosary chapels offer a plenary indulgence to visiting pilgrims.

The Maternity of Mary feast honours the dignity of Mary as Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus solemnly ratified that title on 22 June 431. Its hymns also praise Mary as the spiritual mother of all mankind. The Roman Breviary commemorates it on the second Sunday in October.

Portugal first received the feast in 1751 at the petition of King Joseph Manuel. Venice, Naples, and Tuscany followed it across the next fifty years. Rome keeps it at St Augustine's with a solemn octave each year. At Mesagna it marks the great earthquake of 20 February 1743.

The Most Pure Heart of Mary feast honours Mary's joys, sorrows, virtues, and perfections. John Eudes began it as the patronal feast of his priests and nuns. Kept at Caen from 1644, it spread across nearly all France. Its Office, composed by Eudes, was fixed in text by 1672.

French bishops claimed the right to found feasts and compose offices without Rome's leave. Pius VI gave the first papal sanction to Corbeil nuns in 1787. Rome adopted the feast in 1879, though it never reached the whole Church. Ecuador keeps it as patronal feast of the republic to this day.

The Nativity of Mary falls on 8 September in the Latin Church. Its earliest witness is a sixth-century hymn by St Romanus the Melodist. The feast likely arose in Syria or Palestine soon after the Council of Ephesus. Rome took it in the seventh century from the Eastern churches.

The story of Mary's birth comes only from apocryphal gospels and legends. Many Latin calendars were slow to accept this Eastern festival. Sergius I ordered a litany and procession for the feast day. Innocent IV added an octave after the cardinals' vow in conclave.

The Presentation of Mary recalls her being brought to the Temple aged three. Apocryphal gospels say her parents fulfilled a vow in doing so. The feast arose in the East, likely in Syria, its apocryphal home. A Greek canon for it dates from the seventh or eighth century.

Philippe de Mazieres brought the feast to the West at Avignon. Paris kept it in 1373, Metz in 1418, and Cologne in 1420. Sixtus IV entered it in the Roman Breviary for a time. Sixtus V restored it in 1585, and Rome keeps it as a major double.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feasts-of-the:
The Seven Sorrows feasts honour Mary's spiritual martyrdom standing beneath the Cross beside her Son. One falls on the Friday before Palm Sunday each year. The other falls on the third Sunday in September. Both recall her compassion in Christ's sufferings from Simeon's prophecy to the burial.

The Servites took Mary's sorrows as the chief devotion of their order in 1239. Cologne's synod enacted the feast in 1413 to expiate the crimes of Hussite iconoclasts. Benedict XIII spread the Friday feast to the whole Church in 1727. Pius VII extended the September feast after his exile in 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florence-conr:
Florence Conry was Archbishop of Tuam, patriot, and founder of the Irish College at Louvain. Born in Galway in 1560, he joined the Franciscans at Salamanca and became Irish provincial in 1588. He sailed with the Spanish Armada and later aided Hugh O'Neill in Tyrone's Rebellion. After Kinsale in 1601 he went to Spain with Hugh Roe O'Donnell and stood by the exiled earls.

Consecrated archbishop at Rome in 1609, he never took possession of his see under penal proclamations. In 1616 he founded St. Anthony's College at Louvain, home of Irish scholars and a busy press. He translated a Spanish catechism into pure Irish, printed at Louvain in 1626. A deep scholar of Augustine, he wrote on grace, free will, and original sin until his death in 1629.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-french-congre:
The French Congregation of the Oratory, founded at Paris in 1611 by Cardinal Pierre de Bérulle, aimed to renew the priesthood in France. Bérulle took Saint Philip Neri's Italian Oratory as his model but changed one thing: where Italian houses stood independent, all French houses answered to a single superior-general. A papal bull of 1613 approved the new institute.

More than fifty houses joined during Bérulle's lifetime, and later the count more than doubled across four provinces. Members took no vows beyond priesthood itself, and their one aim was priestly perfection. Though not a teaching order, the Oratorians ran colleges and were the first to shape French seminaries on the lines of the Council of Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gervase-of-ca:
Gervase of Canterbury, an English chronicler born about 1141, wrote the monks' side of Canterbury's quarrels. Of a Kentish family, he took profession from Saint Thomas on February 16, 1163. He was ordained by him and helped bury the saint after his martyrdom on December 29, 1170. He fought Archbishop Baldwin in the monks' disputes of 1185 to 1191, carrying appeals to pope and to Richard I in 1189.

Made sacristan about the time he attended Hubert Walter in 1193, Gervase ceased that office by 1197, when Felix appears as sacristan. He was still writing in 1199, and his Gesta Regum runs to 1210. A sudden change of style and arrangement signals a new chronicler, so his death falls in or soon after that year. His Chronicle of 1100 to 1199 and Acts of Canterbury's Pontiffs to Hubert Walter's death in 1205 appeared in Twysden in 1652. His Gesta Regum and topographical Mappa Mundi appeared in the Rolls Series of 1879 to 1880 under Stubbs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gervase-of-ti:
Gervase of Tilbury, a writer born about 1150, entertained an emperor with the world's wonders. Of Tilbury in Essex, likely kin to English royalty. He served Henry of Guienne, traveled Europe, studied and briefly taught canon law at Bologna, and attended William II of Sicily's court until 1189. Settling at Arles, he became Marshal of the Kingdom of Arles in 1198 under Otto IV, escorting him to Rome's coronation in 1209.

Between 1210 and 1214 Gervase composed Otia Imperialia, also called Book of the World's Marvels, Emperor's Solace, and Description of the Whole World. It ran in three parts on history, geography, and physics. Much read in the Middle Ages and twice rendered into French in the fourteenth century, it divides judges. Leibniz dismissed it as a bag of foolish old wives' tales, while others prize its recognition of papal claims against empire. Leibniz edited it in 1744, and much of Gervase's other writing has perished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glory:
Glory is a word of many shades of meaning, which lexicographers struggle to separate sharply. In the English Bible it translates Hebrew terms of the Old Testament and the Greek doxa of the New Testament. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats it only in its ethical and religious senses, as Scripture and theology use it.

Sometimes it means a visible brightness, as in the glory of the Lord dwelling on Sinai or the Transfiguration on Mount Thabor. Often it means the witness creation bears to its Creator. It can also mean a manifestation of divine majesty through the incarnate Son, as in John 1:14. It also means praise given to God, judgment on personal worth, and finally the blessedness of the future life in union with God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorian-ant:
The Gregorian Antiphonary is an article on the earliest collection of antiphons, groups of antiphons, and their melodies. A primitive Christian antiphonary can no longer be reconstructed completely, but study of the text establishes its existence at a remote date. A Catholic Encyclopedia article distinguishes idiomelodic antiphons, fitted with special melodies, from automelodic anthems adapted to a common type.

The list of melodies was limited. Oral tradition may have sufficed to hand down musical formulas until the chants were coordinated and notation became necessary. From the fourth century singers commonly used a book or page bearing the notation, though many churches had only the words. The oldest trace is an Egyptian papyrus of about the year 300, worn where singers' fingers held it, carrying a Greek text of praise to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hail-mary:
The Hail Mary, also called the Angelical Salutation or Ave Maria, is the most familiar prayer in honour of the Blessed Virgin. The entry traces its three parts to their sources. Gabriel's greeting in Luke supplies the opening, Elizabeth's words add the blessing on the fruit of Mary's womb. The Church itself framed the closing petition for sinners now and at the hour of death.

No firm trace of the prayer as a set formula appears before about 1050, when its phrases surface in the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin. Synods from Paris in 1196 and Durham in 1217 pressed clergy to teach it beside the Creed and Lord's Prayer. Early users treated it as a greeting, kneeling or bowing as they said it, and saints like Louis of France repeated it fifty times nightly on their knees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-fleur:
Hugh of Fleury, also called Hugo a Santa Maria, was a Benedictine monk and church writer known only through his writings, dead not before 1118. In 1109 he compiled a church history in four volumes reaching the death of Charlemagne in 814. The next year he recast it in six volumes, better arranged, with theological notes added and some matter dropped, reaching 855.

That edition, first printed at Münster in 1638, also carries a preface to King Louis the Fat and a letter to Ivo of Chartres. Hugh also wrote a book on the acts of the Frankish kings from 842 to 1108. He wrote a chronicle of French kings from the legendary Pharamond to Philip I. He also wrote an abridged chronicle for Louis VI, and a work on royal and priestly power for Henry II during the investiture controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hungary:
Hungary, the Realm of the Crown of St. Stephen, lay between set longitudes and latitudes in central Europe, joining Hungary Proper and Transylvania with Croatia-Slavonia and the Military Frontier. Its total area was over one hundred and twenty-five thousand square miles, and its 1900 population exceeded nineteen million, just over half Catholic. Budapest, on both banks of the Danube, held about eight hundred thousand people.

The Danube and its tributaries, the Save, Drave, and Theiss, drain the land. Great plains, the Alföld, fill tens of thousands of square miles between Alps and Carpathians. Farming led its industries. The entry then traces Hungary's church history from early conversion through Reformation struggles. Districts beyond the Theiss accepted Reformed religion in 1556, and Catholic revival followed under Archbishop Oláhus, who held a national synod in 1561 and founded a seminary at Tyrnau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idolatry:
The word idolatry first meant divine worship given to an image. Now it covers worship of anything at all: divine worship offered to any being or thing other than the true God. For Aquinas it is a kind of superstition, a vice against religion: it offers divine honour to non-divine things, or to God in a wrong manner. Its specific mark is direct opposition to worship's primary object.

In several ways it hands a creature the reverence owed to God alone. Some, by nefarious arts, made images that seemed, through the devil's power, to work effects, and judged them divine and worthy of worship, as Hermes Trismegistus held. Others honoured not images but the creatures they represented. Paul hints at both in Romans, where people changed God's glory into the likeness of corruptible things.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institute-of-:
Mary Ward's second congregation, founded for the schooling of girls, carries the official title Institute of Mary. After her first congregation was suppressed in 1630 and attacked as “Jesuitesses,” most members left religious life or joined other orders. A loyal group, sheltered at Munich in the Paradeiser Haus with Pope Urban VIII's leave and the Elector of Bavaria's help, kept living under Ward's guidance.

In 1703 Barbara Babthorpe won approval for the institute's rule under this title. She was the fourth successor as chief superior. The title appears in early superiors' signatures and in the first members' formula of vows. In different lands the sisters were known as English Ladies, Dames Anglaises, or Loreto nuns. The entry traces a community that survived suppression by holding fast to its founder's plan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-institu:
Frances Mary Teresa Ball founded this Irish teaching congregation under Dublin's Archbishop Murray, after two years as a novice at St Mary's Convent, York. Ellen Arthur and Anne Therry joined her as the first companions. On 4 November 1822 the three pioneers took possession of Rathfarnham Abbey. The archbishop had bought it as motherhouse and novitiate. Dubliners soon called the sisters Loreto nuns.

Fame for the superior schooling they gave in the Dublin archdiocese drew calls for their help across Ireland. Navan in County Meath took the first offshoot in 1833, with a later filiation at Mullingar, and Dublin houses in North Great George's Street and Stephen's Green followed. The entry traces a teaching order spreading from one abbey to a national network of girls' schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ivory:
Ivory is dentine, the tusk matter of elephants, hippopotami, walruses, and other animals. It is tough and elastic. It holds a creamy white color. It takes a high and lasting polish. Artists have used it since prehistoric times. Early and medieval Christians used it widely for church objects.

Museums in Europe hold carved ivories from many ages. Examples include Egyptian, Assyrian, Greek, and Roman reliefs. They also include statues, diptychs, plaques, and caskets. Classical writers often mention ivory. The Old Testament uses its traits as poetic praise. The Litany of Loreto still calls Mary a tower of ivory. The entry surveys a material prized for beauty and craft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-andre:
Jacques André Emery led the Society of St Sulpice through the French Revolution. He was born at Gex on 26 August 1732. He died at Paris on 28 April 1811. He studied first with Carmelites at Gex and Jesuits at Mâcon. He then attended St Irenaeus seminary at Lyons. He finished at St Sulpice, Paris, joined the society, and was ordained priest in 1758.

He taught with distinction at Orléans and Lyons seminaries. At Lyons he defended Rome's rights firmly yet courteously before Archbishop de Montazet, a Jansenist-leaning prelate. Partly on that archbishop's advice, he became superior at Angers seminary in 1776. Later he became vicar-general of the diocese. He showed marked governing power in both posts. In 1782 he was elected superior-general of St Sulpice. The entry follows a seminary chief steering priests through revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-de-vi:
Historian of the crusades Jacques de Vitry was cardinal bishop of Acre, later of Tusculum. He was born at Vitry-sur-Seine near Paris, probably about 1160, and died at Rome in 1240. After attending Paris university in its infancy, he visited Marie d'Oignies, a Liège mystic famed for holiness. On her advice he became a canon regular. He returned to Paris for priestly ordination and then devoted himself to preaching.

From 1210 to 1213 he ranked among the most noted preachers of the crusade against the Albigenses. His fame spread so widely that Acre's Latin clergy chose him as bishop. He accepted with Honorius III's approval. From Palestine he went to Egypt and witnessed Damietta's capture in 1218 to 1220. He wrote an account of it to the pope. Crusade leaders complained of his imperious temper and ambition. The entry follows a preacher become bishop on crusading frontiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-joseph-:
Third bishop of Hamilton, Ontario, James Joseph Carbery was born in County Westmeath, Ireland, on 1 May 1823, and died at Cork on 17 December 1887. Early education at Navan seminary led him into the Dominican order at an early age. Philosophy and theology at Viterbo and Rome prepared a return to Ireland in 1849. There he soon became known for learning, eloquence, and zealous labors.

Many important posts in his order followed, including assistant to the master general, and in 1883 he was appointed bishop of Hamilton, consecrated at Rome on 11 November that year. He died while visiting his native country to restore his broken health, a Dominican scholar-bishop whose Canadian episcopate lasted only four years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-mcsherr:
James McSherry served as chief justice of Maryland's highest court from 25 January 1896 until his death, with distinction, among the state's judges of the postwar generation. In 1887 he had become chief judge of the circuit court for Frederick and Montgomery counties, a post that carried a seat on the appeals court. Voters gave him a full term with no rival on the ballot on 8 November 1887.

His father was the author James McSherry. The younger man was born in Frederick, Maryland, on 30 December 1842, and died there on 23 October 1907. Mount St Mary's College in Emmitsburg schooled him until the year before graduation, when his open Southern views got him sent away in 1861. Arrested, he spent a spell confined at Fort McHenry in Baltimore. He then learned law beside his father and qualified as a lawyer on 8 February 1864. Clara Louise McAleer became his wife on 26 February 1866, and they raised six children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-g:
Jean-Pierre Gury, a French Jesuit moral theologian born in 1801 and dead in 1866. He joined the Society at Montrouge in 1824 and taught moral theology for thirty-five years, mainly at Vals seminary, with one year at Rome. His teaching career shaped generations of confessors.

Gury's Compendium of Moral Theology, first issued in 1850, reached seventeen editions by his death. Confession, or The Blind Heart, a domestic story by W Gilmore Simms, opens under a motto from Goethe's Faust about those who knew and felt, and were crucified or burnt for telling. Simms begins by repeating the quotation and turning it into an essay. The pains and penalties of folly, he argues, are not necessarily death. The old texts threatened as much, but life is subtler. The blind heart of his title is the organ that refuses its own knowledge.

From that somber porch the tale enters Southern domestic life, where a confession withheld or mistimed poisons a household. Simms works here in the domestic vein: marriage, conscience, family honor. Kolliker's rival Theory of Heterogeneous Generation gets the closer handling, first in its objections and then in its construction. Huxley charges him with mistaking Darwin for a teleologist, a thinker who builds purpose into nature. Varieties, Huxley insists, arise by general laws whether useful, hurtful, or indifferent. The essay is Darwin's bulldog at work in print: part summary, part cross-examination, part counter-attack.

The future was biorefinery. The data were energy. The ReSOURCE were future. The negative were carbon. The energy were folks.

The technologies were energy-efficient. The data were energy. The Mexico were cooling. The US were assessment.
doe-osti-3374538-advanced-test-reactor-n: ATR got dosimetry-reported, and this DOE report covers 174 A and B. The pages detail the neutron findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The reactor was advanced test. The data were nuclear. The 174 were dosimetry. The test were advanced.

The energy folks get their closeout. The evaluation was quantitative. The closeout was energy. The imagery were fleet. The quantitative were evaluation.
doe-osti-3415860-a-synthetic-photonic-do: When blasts throw dust and debris through the air, clocking their speed is brutally hard. This work builds a synthetic testbed for photonic Doppler velocimetry — a laser method that reads velocity — tuned for particle-filled flows. The numerical framework lets researchers check their instruments against known answers.
dream-life-and-real-life-a-little-africa:
Olive Schreiner called Dream Life and Real Life a little African story, dedicating it to her brother Fred, for whose school magazine its first tiny tale was written years before. The 1893 Eastbourne dedication dates the collection. A glossary first explains the karoo landscape. Kopjes rise like ruined castles there. Kraals, krantzes, and sluits carrying storm water complete the picture.

Three stories follow. The title tale concerns a child on a karoo farm. The Woman's Rose remembers white acacia flowers gathered by a man's strong hand on a sultry afternoon. A piece on protection policy closes the set. Schreiner's South African childhood supplies the heat, stones, and loneliness. These early pieces show her allegorical gift forming.
eben-holden-a-tale-of-the-north-country:
Irving Bacheller dated his preface April 1900 and built this tale from the Vermont settlers who crossed into the Adirondack wilderness of northern New York. The preface sketches their world: stumpy farms, coon-skin coats, and sons raised on honour, industry, and the hope of being president. The story itself opens with a ruined Vermont home and a strange little expedition west.

A small boy rides in a basket on the back of a jolly old man, Eben Holden. Holden carries a cane in one hand and a rifle in the other, with a black dog for scout. The boy narrates their life in the north country as he grows. Newspaper editor Horace Greeley enters the tale in its later chapters, from files and memories Bacheller acknowledges in his preface.
from-wealth-to-poverty-or-the-tricks-of-:
Austin Potter's From Wealth to Poverty, or The Tricks of the Traffic, is a temperance story subtitled A Story of the Drink Curse. Potter dedicates it to prohibition's friends around the world. His preface names two motives: hatred of the rum traffic, and a desire to expose the liquor party's measures against the Dunkin Act.

Potter writes from personal experience and observation, having lived in three counties where drink brought hardship to himself and those dear to him. The story follows a family's fall from wealth to poverty, showing how the traffic's tricks ensnare its victims. Readers interested in the temperance movement, or in Victorian moral fiction with a reforming edge, will find Potter earnest and unsparing.
geronimo-story:
Geronimo, the Apache war leader, dictated his life story in 1906 while held as a prisoner of war at Fort Sill. S. M. Barrett, a local school official, took down his words with his permission. Geronimo said he wanted the truth told at last.

He recalls his youth in the Southwest, Mexican raids that killed his family, and his long wars against Mexico and the United States. His surrenders, escapes, and final capture in 1886 close the tale. The book gives the Apache wars from the Apache side, in a voice both proud and bitter. Geronimo died still a prisoner three years later.
glengarry-school-days-a-story-of-early-d:
Ralph Connor wrote Glengarry School Days as a novel of pioneer schooling in Glengarry, a Scottish settlement district in eastern Ontario, Canada. Its setting is the Twentieth school, a log building ringed by deep forest. Master Archibald Munro rules the room with a lame knee, a firm hand, and surprising fairness. Hughie Murray, the minister's lively son, stands near the center of the children's world.

Chapters move from a Friday spelling match to examinations, a new master, and a bear hunt in the woods. Pranks, fights, and loyalty tests fill the school year. Foxy and his partner scheme, Hughie wins a measure of freedom, and two hard rounds settle old scores. Connor gives readers a warm, rough picture of settlement childhood, where lessons in books mattered less than courage, honesty, and standing by friends.
god-s-good-man-a-simple-love-story:
Marie Corelli dedicated God's Good Man to the living original of her hero. The Reverend John Walden and his wife receive the book as a simple love story, affectionately given. Her epigraph runs that there was a man sent from God whose name was John. The novel opens in an English May after a cruel winter.

Walden, a saintly country parson, loves Maryllia, a wealthy woman who returns to her ancestral village. Church politics, a scheming squire, and village gossip oppose their union. Corelli contrasts Walden's pure ministry with worldly clergy who serve fashion. Spring blossom, cowslips, and bluebells frame her sermons in story form. The book was among her best loved, read as both romance and rebuke. Her good man stands against an age she thought faithless and greedy.
govdocs-archive_org-JonBenetRamseyCaseSu:
Chapter twenty of David McGowan's Programmed to Kill, titled Boulder, treats the murder of JonBenet Ramsey, the six-year-old found dead in her Boulder, Colorado home in 1996. McGowan's book argues that many notorious crimes hide organized abuse networks. The Ramsey chapter applies that thesis to America's most debated unsolved case.

McGowan reviews the ransom note, the family's conduct, the police work, and the media storm, reading each through his characteristic conspiratorial lens. His account is argument, not established fact; the case remains officially unsolved and widely disputed. The chapter is held as true-crime writing from the archive, for researchers who study the case and its literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HaapinenLarry_H:
Larry Haapinen wrote an article titled Oswald and the U-2, pegged to Francis Gary Powers' book Operation Overflight. Powers was the U-2 pilot shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960. Haapinen's piece discusses Lee Harvey Oswald in connection with the U-2 affair.

Oswald had served as a Marine radar operator and later defected to the Soviet Union, which long fed questions about what he knew. Tying his name to the spy plane story placed the assassin inside Cold War intelligence history. The article preserves that line of speculation as it was argued in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HurtHenry_Hurt_:
Chapter Eleven of Henry Hurt's book on the Kennedy assassination takes up the Cuban question. Its title asks the book's central choice: coincidence or conspiracy. In the chapter Hurt quotes the Schweiker Report, a Senate product, and President Lyndon B. Johnson himself.

Cuba sat at the crossroads of the case: Castro's enemies, Oswald's pro-Castro acts, and exile raiders all met there. Hurt weighs whether those crossings were chance or design. A senator's report and a president's words give the chapter its spine, and the excerpt preserves his argument at its most pointed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PetersenHenry_P:
FBI official A. Evans sent this memorandum to Mr. Belmont on December 17, 1963. Its subject is Henry Petersen of the Justice Department. Petersen worked in the department's Organized Crime and Racketeering Section. He had been asked to serve on the Presidential Commission investigating the Kennedy assassination, the body soon known as the Warren Commission.

Staffing the commission was sensitive work. A Justice Department organized-crime man brought one kind of expertise and one kind of suspicion. The memo records the bureau noting the appointment for its own files. It is a small dated trace of the commission being assembled, less than a month after the assassination, while the FBI watched who would judge its work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StoneGregory_St: Los Angeles police oversight took place in public, and the meeting of March 4, 1986, was written down word for word. The transcript covers item 3-A on the agenda of the LAPD Board of Police Commissioners. Verbatim records like this one show how civilian commissioners questioned and directed one of the largest police departments in the country during the 1980s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Treasury_Treasu: Picture Scoop magazine previewed its contents on a single page, and one item stands out: Henry Morgenthau Jr. writing on Your Money. Morgenthau had been Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of the Treasury. A contents page is only a promise of articles, but it shows how a photo magazine sold financial advice from a famous name. The November page survives as a small piece of magazine history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-UnderhillGary_U: J. Garrett Underhill, a former intelligence agent, told friends he knew who killed President Kennedy. Shortly afterward he was shot dead. The article reporting his death treats it as part of the assassination mystery rather than a closed case. Underhill's story became one of the most repeated in assassination research. The piece preserves the claim and the grim end that made it famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WPAFilmLibrary_: A Christmas card from MPI Media Group reached Harold Weisberg from his friends at the company. MPI worked with film libraries, including the WPA Film Library named in the file. The card is a small, warm item in a research archive mostly filled with conflict and suspicion. It shows the friendly business ties behind Weisberg's later work in film and publishing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WegrockiHenry_W: A Baltimore Sun article by Isaac Rehert profiles a young researcher named Henry Wegrocki. Its headline states his belief plainly: the CIA was behind Kennedy's death. Few newspapers gave young critics of the Warren Commission that kind of space in those years. The article shows a mainstream paper presenting a heretical claim through the person who held it, rather than endorsing or crushing it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
A Colombian taxi driver carried secret cash from Chiquita Brands to a right-wing paramilitary group, and in 2023 he received a thirty-six-month prison sentence. This briefing book, posted that April, draws on internal documents from the Archive's Chiquita Papers. They show his role was larger than earlier reports said.

During the 1990s the driver served as a key go-between for the fruit company. He dealt with practically every major armed actor in Colombia's conflict, not just one group. His case turns an abstract corporate crime into a human chain of payments, one bag of cash at a time.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: The United States and Cyberspace: Military Organization, Policy - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_indonesi:
East Timor voted on independence from Indonesia in a historic 1999 referendum. Brad Simpson edited this briefing book, number 682, marking twenty years since that vote. Declassified documents show what the United States knew in the run-up, and what it chose to protect.

Washington knew the Indonesian military had created, directed, and armed the militias terrorizing East Timor. Their plan was to kill, drive out, or silence independence activists before the vote. Even so, the United States sought to preserve close ties with that military. The gap between knowledge and policy is documented here in the government's own paper.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Anatoly Chernyaev worked inside the Soviet Central Committee and kept a diary that recorded the system talking to itself. Anna Melyakova translated and Svetlana Savranskaya edited this volume, number 830, published in May 2023. The diary covers the year 1983.

Chernyaev complained of his humiliating role, dressing a naked, completely naked king. On the KAL airliner shootdown that year, he wrote that it showcased the power of the military complex over Soviet life and politics. On nuclear war he reflected that a world of human achievement could vanish in a few short minutes. Few sources put a senior insider's private honesty on paper this plainly.

Anatoly Sergeyevich Chernyaev wrote one of the great insider diaries of the late Soviet Union. The Archive published his diary for 1978 in English for the first time in May 2018, on what would have been his ninety-seventh birthday. Svetlana Savranskaya edited the edition.

Chernyaev wrote from inside the Central Committee of the Communist Party, where he then worked. A daily diary at that level records meetings, moods, and doubts that official minutes hide. The 1978 volume predates his years as Gorbachev's aide, which makes it a baseline: the same sharp observer, watching a system that did not yet know it was entering its final decade.

President Bill Clinton traveled to Moscow in January 1994 for a summit with Russian president Boris Yeltsin, barely two years after the Soviet Union collapsed. The National Security Archive briefing book on that meeting publishes declassified transcripts of what the two leaders said to each other behind closed doors.

The talks show close work together on nuclear safety and on regional security problems left over from the Cold War. At the same time, worry grows in the record about Russia's troubled shift to a market system, which was bringing hardship and political strain. Readers see a hopeful partnership in plain language, along with the early signs of the troubles that would later strain it.

Anatoly Chernyaev's diary for 1980 records life inside the Soviet Central Committee while Leonid Brezhnev still ruled. Briefing Book number 706, published in May 2020, presents the diary in Anna Melyakova's translation, edited by Svetlana Savranskaya. The Archive calls its author irreplaceable as a witness to that closed world.

One entry asks who is supposed to answer for Afghanistan, where Soviet troops had invaded the year before. Another notes that most work was done to please one man, Brezhnev, and to disturb him as little as possible. Lines like those show a system run for the comfort of an aging leader. The diary gives readers a rare insider's daily record from behind the Kremlin's walls.

Anatoly Chernyaev wrote his 1984 diary while still waiting for a leader who would change the Soviet Union; Mikhail Gorbachev would take power the next year. Briefing Book number 860 presents that diary, translated and edited by Svetlana Savranskaya with help from Anna Melyakova, as part of the Archive's long project of publishing Chernyaev's private record.

Entries quoted from the diary ask what would happen if the weapons were simply destroyed, full stop. Others call the Afghan war an effort to make a country happy that cost thousands of lives and brought global shame. Chernyaev mocks his own idealism, then sizes up Gorbachev as lively, quick, and able to grasp the essence of things. Few sources show the mood inside the Soviet elite so plainly on the eve of reform.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_colombia-chiquita: Chiquita, the banana company, was found liable in an American court for killings carried out by a Colombian paramilitary group it had paid for years. A National Security Archive briefing book page carries that verdict under a plain headline naming the company and the crime. The case grew from payments Chiquita admitted making to the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, a group on the United States terrorist list. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, marking the Archive's record of a landmark corporate accountability judgment.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-human-rights:
In a forced disappearance case from Bolivia, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ordered the state to open its military archives and guarantee the right to truth. A National Security Archive news post from January 2023 reports the ruling and what it requires of the Bolivian government.

Forced disappearance works by erasing records: the victim vanishes and the state denies everything. An order to open military files attacks that erasure directly, because the archives are where orders, rosters, and reports survive. The court's demand also sets a standard other countries in the region can be measured against. Readers interested in how international courts turn human rights language into concrete duties will find a clear, compact example here.
haste-and-waste-or-the-young-pilot-of-la:
Oliver Optic's Haste and Waste is a story for young people about a young pilot on Lake Champlain. Optic was the pen name of William Taylor Adams, a Boston schoolteacher. He spent twenty years among boys and became one of America's most prolific writers for the young.

The tale belongs to the world of boats, lakeside towns and boy heroes that made Optic's name. Its hero's hurried choices, as the title warns, bring waste and trouble in their train. Adams wrote it in the same plain, energetic style as his Boat Club series, aiming to hold a young reader's attention while rewarding steady character. The front matter sketches Adams's life and long list of books, a reminder of how widely his stories travelled in their day.
hero-tales-from-american-history:
Henry Cabot Lodge and Theodore Roosevelt divided Hero Tales from American History between them, dedicating the book to the friend who suggested it. Their purpose, stated in the preface, is to tell in simple fashion of Americans whose deeds proved their truth in life and in death. Plato's Menexenus supplies the motto about fighting for liberty.

Lodge takes Washington, Trenton, Bennington, Gouverneur Morris, and the burning of the Philadelphia. Roosevelt answers with Daniel Boone, George Rogers Clark, King's Mountain, Stony Point, and the cruise of the Wasp. David Crockett's journey south to Texas fills a later chapter. Two future statesmen wrote these tales for boys, and their idea of heroism, strenuous and patriotic, shaped a generation.
hunter-quatermain-s-story:
H. Rider Haggard built this short tale around his famous white hunter, Allan Quatermain. It opens at the Yorkshire home of Sir Henry Curtis, where the talk turns to the great diamond treasure the men found in Africa. Curtis and Captain Good refuse to tell that story again and call on their old companion instead.

Quatermain, lately back from Africa, obliges with a hunting story from his years on the frontier. The adventure he chooses is a single dangerous stalk that nearly ends him, told plainly and without swagger. Haggard keeps the frame snug and lets the tale stand on close calls, bush craft, and the hunter's dry way of judging men and beasts. Readers who know Quatermain from the novels meet him here at fireside scale, in one evening's telling.
icelandic-primer-with-grammar-notes-and-:
Henry Sweet's An Icelandic Primer, in its second edition of 1895, teaches Old Icelandic with grammar, notes, and a glossary. Sweet's preface says the want of a short, easy introduction had been felt from the beginning of the study in England. Vigfusson and Powell's Icelandic Reader left room for an elementary book. Sweet modelled his on his own Anglo-Saxon primer.

The grammar leans on Noreen's Altisländische Grammatik, which Sweet calls by far the best yet written. His spelling keeps traditional normalized forms, with diacritics supplied where manuscripts are defective. Texts chosen are easy, interesting, and representative, his preface promises. Sweet, the great phonetician, built the primer to lure students of Old English northward. Generations learned their first Icelandic from it. Its clarity made a saga language approachable in a school term, which was precisely the revolution Sweet intended.
in-the-pecos-country:
In the Pecos Country, by Edward Sylvester Ellis writing as Lieutenant R H Jayne, is a frontier adventure set in New Mexico and Texas. Ellis opens in the valley of the Rio Pecos, where New England families under Caleb Barnwell have planted a settlement they christen New Boston. Their leader, part dreamer and part Don Quixote, passed richer and safer land by to settle where the government could barely protect its own citizens.

Barnwell held odd social theories, and rumors of gold and silver along the river may have helped persuade his followers. Chapter headings then tighten the trap: Fred goes on guard, faces Lone Wolf, and the Apaches are coming. The Pecos country, Ellis warns, was then among the most dangerous ground in Indian country. A boy's watch duty, a settlement's stores, and a war party's approach drive this dime novel machinery at full speed.
in-the-sweet-dry-and-dry:
Christopher Morley and Bart Haley's In the Sweet Dry and Dry is a comic novel of Prohibition, signed from Philadelphia ten minutes before midnight on June 30, 1919. That was the last hour before wartime prohibition fell on America. The authors wish their readers a Merry Abstinence and dedicate the book to G. K. Chesterton, most delightful of modern Decanterbury pilgrims. Their foreword begs that no deductions be made about their private habits. The story leaps into a dry future of mysterious juleps and thirsty secrets.

Inside, Morley's Bishop of the future and his flock scheme for liquor in a republic of raids, passwords, and medicinal fictions. The satire is gentle and thirsty rather than angry. Readers get the wittiest period piece of the dry years, two journalists drinking in print on the night the taps closed.
in-wicklow-and-west-kerry:
John M. Synge gathered In Wicklow and West Kerry from articles printed in the Manchester Guardian and the Shanachie. The volume, issued in 1912 after his death, joins two Irish journeys. Wicklow, south of Dublin, supplies the first set of sketches. West Kerry, on the Atlantic edge, supplies the second.

Synge walks with vagrants who have tramped the Wicklow roads for generations. He writes of the oppression of the hills, the people of the glens, and a fair day crowd. A landlord's garden and the valley of Glencree receive quieter studies. His prose listens closely to peasant speech and storytelling. Readers meet an Ireland of workhouses, small farms, and stubborn character, recorded by a playwright with an ear for how people actually talk.
jeff-briggs-s-love-story:
Bret Harte opened Jeff Briggs's Love Story on a storm night at Eldridge's Crossing, where Jeff Briggs keeps the ramshackle Half-way House. Wind and rain batter the loose shutters while the landlord reads himself to sleep in his attic, until a gaunt woman in a plaid shawl taps at his door. The visitor brings the past with her, and with it the love story of the title, told back through Jeff's rough California years.

Harte frames the tale as a confidence made in bad weather: how a stage-stop keeper loved, lost, and kept the memory. His California of inns, crossings, and sudden guests supplies the weather and the people. It is a quieter Harte piece, built on voice and retrospect rather than gold-camp incident.
jewish-history-an-essay-in-the-philosoph:
Simon Dubnow's Jewish History is an essay on the philosophy of history, by a leading Russian-Jewish historian. The sample carries the preface written for its German translation. That preface calls Dubnow's place in Russian-Jewish writing almost dominant. It praises his studies of Polish-Russian Jews and of Hasidism as work of lasting weight.

The preface stresses how Dubnow writes, not only what he covers. It joins strict scholarly care with warm feeling and clear, shaped prose. Dubnow held that dullness is no duty of scholarship, and that dry writing faults the writer, not the subject. His aim was to give each fact its place in the line of growth, linking Jewish history with mankind's history.
jim-cummings-or-the-great-adams-express-:
Jim Cummings, or The Great Adams Express Robbery, is a detective tale by A. Frank Pinkerton. It appeared as volume one of the Pinkerton Detective Series, issued monthly from Chicago in March 1887. The book carries a portrait of the notorious Jim Cummings. It also prints scenes tied to the great robbery of its title.

Chapter one opens in a back room behind a Chicago coal office on West Lake Street. Three men sit around a pine table with curtains drawn and a blanket nailed over the door. Maps, railroad time-tables, and pens cover the table. One big man practices writing the name J. B. Barrett again and again. The forged letter and the plan, the chapter heading promises, are taking shape.
kincaid-s-battery:
Kincaid's Battery is George Washington Cable's novel of New Orleans in the Civil War, published in 1908. Alonzo Kimball illustrated it, and Cable inscribes it to E.C.S.C. Thirteen chapters run from Carrollton Gardens to The General's Standard. The general's choice and battery manoeuvres set the military frame early.

One killed and the fight for the standard raise the cost of the battery's honor. Flora, Anna, Constance, and Kincaid each carry chapters named for their turns. Charlie races for Anna, and Anna and Adolphe meet at the corner. A duel, a recall, and the naming of Kincaid's battery close the contents. Cable, the Louisiana novelist, writes of Creole New Orleans divided by war and bound by its codes of honor.
king-alfred-of-england-makers-of-history:
King Alfred of England is Jacob Abbott's biography of Alfred the Great, in his Makers of History series. Harper and Brothers entered the book in 1849. Abbott's preface states the series' aim: a clear and connected narrative of each subject's life. He adds moral lessons drawn from the story, in a direct and simple style.

Abbott believed such lives could interest mature minds as much as young readers. Alfred's story gives him rich matter: a king who fought the Danes and fostered learning. The series made great lives into schoolroom and family reading across America. This volume presents Alfred as scholar, warrior, and lawgiver in Abbott's plain, steady manner. It served generations of young readers as their first Alfred.
laddie-a-true-blue-story:
Gene Stratton-Porter's novel Laddie calls itself a true blue story. She dedicated it to Leander Elliot Stratton. Its motto says the way to be happy is to be good.

A character list opens the book, led by Laddie himself. Chapters move from Little Sister and a first day of school to weddings and Christmas. A Pryor family mystery threads through the later chapters. Stratton-Porter sets the tale in a warm rural home. Faith, family love, and honest work guide its young hero through trouble. A princess, a pie, and a homing pigeon appear in chapter titles. Such touches keep the family story light between its trials.
little-memoirs-of-the-nineteenth-century:
George Paston published these brief memoirs in 1902. Paston was the pen name of Emily Morse Symonds. The preface chooses minor celebrities of the nineteenth century. Their experiences illustrate literary and artistic life especially.

Paston favors figures not yet overwhelmed by minor biographers. Two foreigners join the group for an outsider's verdict. Pückler-Muskau and N. P. Willis observed English manners freshly. Nearly all subjects were born in the late eighteenth century. All heroes and heroines but one were born after 1775. A previous volume treated the eighteenth century the same way.
lovey-mary:
Lovey Mary is a novel by Alice Hegan Rice, published in 1903. Rice had just won fame with Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch. Her dedication thanks her husband Cale Young Rice for his secret of plucking roses. The story returns to the Cabbage Patch, a poor city settlement.

Lovey Mary is an orphan girl with a warm, stubborn heart. Chapters bring a runaway couple, a Labor Day, and a Christmas play. The cactus plant of the first chapter blooms by the last. Rice writes of poor neighbors with humor and deep kindness. The book mixes tears and laughter in her beloved style.
manual-for-noncommissioned-officers-and-:
The Manual for Noncommissioned Officers and Privates of Infantry dates from 1917. The War Department issued it as Document Number 574. It was approved at Washington on April 14, 1917, days after America entered the war. Engineer and Coast Artillery companies also used it for infantry training.

Chapter one lays down military discipline and courtesy. Sections cover the oath of enlistment, obedience, and loyalty. Saluting gets its own rules, spelled out in fine detail. Drill, guard duty, and camp life fill the chapters after. The manual put one standard into every soldier's hands. It shows the citizen army of 1917 learning its trade.
maria-chapdelaine-a-tale-of-the-lake-st-:
Maria Chapdelaine is Louis Hémon's tale of the Lake St. John country. W. H. Blake translated it, and Macmillan printed it at New York in 1921. Edition after edition followed through 1922, a sure sign of success. The first chapter names Peribonka, the village of Maria's home.
