The Chapdelaines farm a clearing cut from the wild northern forest. François passes by, and vows are made under the northern sky. Maria must choose between the land's hard call and an easier life. Snow, church bells, and backbreaking work fill her seasons. Hémon wrote French Canada's most beloved novel of the soil. Its plain, strong beauty has never faded.
mary-prince-history:
Mary Prince dictated The History of Mary Prince in London in 1831. She was the first enslaved Black woman to publish a life narrative in Britain. Anti-slavery allies printed her words while her case stirred public debate.

Prince tells of slavery in Bermuda and Antigua: salt ponds, beatings, and masters who blocked her marriage and her freedom. She came to England as a servant and refused to return to bondage. Her plain account of pain and labor shocked British readers. The book struck a real blow for abolition in the last years before emancipation in the colonies.
mary-slessor-of-calabar-pioneer-missiona:
W. P. Livingstone wrote Mary Slessor of Calabar: Pioneer Missionary. His first note sets out the kind of life he means to tell. Slessor, he says, broke rules and followed ideals, not mere routine.

She meant to write her own tale, but died before she could. Livingstone built the book from her letters and many other sources. He praises her self denial, her courage, and her power over fierce folk. Yet he notes her shyness, her fears, and her plain, childlike faith. He warns that no sketch can hold her full, mixed nature. That frank note makes the praise that follows ring more true.
mcclellan-own-story:
George McClellan, the Union general who built the Army of the Potomac, died before finishing his memoir. McClellan's Own Story appeared in 1887, set in order by his literary executor. It is his defense of his Civil War command.

McClellan tells of the Peninsula campaign, Antietam, and his removal by Lincoln. He insists that Washington starved him of men and misread the enemy. Critics have long disputed his claims, which is part of the book's interest. Few Civil War memoirs show so clearly how a general argues his case to history. His widow saw the unfinished work through the press after his death.
men-of-invention-and-industry:
Samuel Smiles wrote these biographical sketches of British inventors and engineers. Each chapter takes up one maker or one trade. Subjects include shipbuilder Phineas Pett and John Harrison, inventor of the marine chronometer. Other chapters cover the screw propeller, the silk trade, and steam printing.

Smiles tells each life as a lesson in patience, thrift, and steady work. He follows printers like Koenig and Clowes as they mechanized the book trade. A closing section looks at industry in Ireland, including coach operator Charles Bianconi. The book captures Victorian faith that character, more than genius, drives invention.
michael-brother-of-jerry:
Jack London published this dog novel in 1917, as a companion to Jerry of the Islands. Its hero is Michael, an Irish terrier and Jerry's brother. London opens with a long foreword about trained animals. He says he learned early to look behind every animal act for the cruelty that produced it.

The foreword argues that deliberate cruelty reaches its worst form in the training ring. London lists the horrors he witnessed in slums, prisons, and battlefields, yet ranks stage training as colder. The novel then follows Michael through the world of ships and show business. It asks readers to see performing animals as victims, not amusements.
mistress-and-maid-a-household-story:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik published this household story under the name Miss Muloch. This Richmond edition appeared in 1864. The tale opens as the three Leaf sisters debate a revolution: hiring a servant. Their new maid is a tall, awkward girl of fifteen, daughter of a widowed washerwoman named Mrs. Hand.

The sisters have long done everything themselves. Hilary, the youngest, teaches school, cooks dinner, and scrubs floors, ruining her pretty hands. Selina is often ill, and Leaf is aging. Craik, who wrote John Halifax, Gentleman, turns domestic service into a study of class, duty, and sisterly sacrifice.
mosaics-of-grecian-history:
Marcius Willson and Robert Pierpont Willson wrote this history of Greece for general readers. Their preface declares its object: a trustworthy history within moderate compass, and an interesting one. They attack the standard school manuals, mere abridgments and outlines. Outlines, they argue, invert the natural order of learning and make history drudgery.

People actually read legends, romances, poems, and biographies, the Willsons note. Shakespeare's plays, they claim, taught the public more English history than all formal tomes. They quote Macaulay approving a touch of fiction's exaggeration in history. Their mosaic pieces Greek cities, wars, and philosophers into vivid fragments a beginner can enjoy.
mother-a-story:
Kathleen Norris opens this story in a village schoolroom during a storm. Margaret Paget has taught there nearly four years, since her seventeenth birthday. Snow has turned to rain, and muddy streams run through the schoolhouse yard. Margaret knows every feature of the big bare room by heart.

Norris dedicates the book with a poem about bringing tales to a mother's knees. The title promises the theme: a woman's life given to mothering. Margaret's years at the window, in all weathers, frame a story of patience and sacrifice. Norris became one of America's most popular novelists of domestic life, and this early book shows why.
mouser-cat-s-story:
Amy Prentice wrote this children's story, illustrated by J. Watson Davis with thirty-five pictures. A color frontispiece shows Mrs. Mouser Cat carrying a mouse to Aunt Amy. The frame opens on a stormy day. Aunt Amy, kept idle by illness, sits lonely by the window, sure no animal friend will visit in such weather.

Then Mrs. Mouser Cat speaks from the doorway, for the first time ever. She scolds Aunt Amy for not caring whether Mrs. Man makes the pickles properly. Aunt Amy, astonished, finds a new storyteller. Prentice's animal tales let each creature narrate its own life, and the cat takes her turn here.
mr-world-and-miss-church-member-a-twenti:
W. S. Harris, a minister, wrote this allegory in twenty-five chapters. Its title pairs Mr. World with Miss Church-Member. Harris says critics read the draft and helped polish it. Paul Krafft of New York drew the pictures.

The tale works like a modern Pilgrim's Progress. Mr. World courts the church member and lures her toward ease. Worldly fashion and pleasure test her faith step by step. Harris aims the lesson at churchgoers of his own day. He feared new morals were pulling believers from strict paths. The book states its moral truths in story form, plainly and with zeal.
nasa-tm-19650017032-a-wind-tunnel-invest:
Robert T Taylor and William J Alford Jr at Langley tested small models of two famous aircraft together in December 1959. One model was the X-15 rocket plane, at one-fortieth scale. The other was its B-52 carrier aircraft. In real flights, the B-52 carried the X-15 aloft before release.

Taylor and Alford measured the carry loads between the pair. They also measured how each aircraft disturbed the air for the other. That mutual interference affects loads at the moment of release. Tunnel data on models let the team study a risky moment safely, before any crew flew it for real.
nasa-tm-19660014308-saturn-i-summary:
A narrative summary of the Saturn I launch vehicle fills this volume, from its start in 1958 through 1965. It is told as a story, not a data report. The prologue opens with the old dream of space travel, noting a fictional Moon voyage written by the year 160. Flying chariots, wings, and rides with angels fill the early pages, before real rockets enter.

Then the account turns to Saturn I itself, with its development and mission highlights. A photograph of the fifth Saturn I rising opens the surviving sample. Program summaries like this one were written for a broad audience. They preserve how the Saturn team told its own story while the larger Saturn V was still being built.
nasa-tm-19670008944-the-atmosphere-of-me:
S. I. Rasool, S. H. Gross, and W. E. McGovern wrote this paper on the atmosphere of Mercury in January 1966. Rasool and McGovern worked at New York University and NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York. Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, and whether it holds any air at all was then an open question.

The review moves from early visual observations of the planet to recent radar measurements. It weighs the evidence for an atmosphere from polarimetric and spectroscopic studies. Temperature measurements from infrared and microwave work come next. A central problem follows: Mercury's weak gravity lets gases escape thermally, and the solar wind strips more away. Closing sections build models of the atmosphere's thermal structure, from the lower layers up through the thermosphere and exosphere.
nasa-tm-19670009385-the-capillary-instab:
N. K. Nayyar and a colleague, both visiting NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center from the University of Delhi in India, study a liquid jet in this paper. The jet carries an electric current along its axis. Their question is how stable such a jet is against the pinching forces that break jets into drops.

They investigate the instability for varicose deformations, the bulging mode of the jet. Their analysis includes the Hall current in Ohm's law. Including it, they find, makes the jet less stable, though with a small frequency of oscillation. The result bears on liquid-metal flows proposed for space power systems.
nasa-tm-19680016463-exploring-in-aerospa:
Exploring in Aerospace Rocketry records a Lewis Research Center program for select high school students, run in 1966 and 1967 under advisor James F. Connors. Director Abe Silverstein started the Lewis Aerospace Explorer Post in December 1965. Principals at seven local high schools picked boys, ages fifteen to nineteen, who showed skill and interest in math and science.

The post took students out of the classroom and into the real world of aerospace engineering. Its stated aims were career guidance and fresh drive toward technical and professional work in the field. Sessions showed the young men the skills, planning, and teamwork behind a successful mission. The volume preserves how NASA introduced itself to a future generation of engineers.
nasa-tm-19680024835-on-the-thermal-radio:
Yu. N. Vetukhnovskaya and A. D. Kuzmin, of the P. N. Lebedev Physical Institute in Moscow, wrote this study of Mercury's thermal radio emission. Issued in Russian in 1967 and translated in June 1968, it reads the planet's heat through radio telescopes. The measured glow, called brightness temperature, varies with sunlight phase and with the wavelength observed.

The authors argue such readings can reveal Mercury's temperature pattern and the heat and electrical traits of its surface soil. Night side readings in infrared light carry special weight, they note. Because Mercury's sunlight far exceeds the Moon's and swings widely, lunar theory cannot simply be copied. The paper therefore builds Mercury's own thermal model and compares theory with experiment.
nasa-tm-19690026544-the-magnetic-structu:
Norman F. Ness, of Goddard Space Flight Center's Laboratory for Space Sciences, wrote this August 1969 paper, X-616-69-334. He summarizes present understanding of the magnetic structure of interplanetary space. Since 1962, spacecraft had measured the region between Venus's orbit and beyond Earth's. They confirmed a continuous flow of plasma from the Sun, the solar wind that Parker had predicted.

A very weak magnetic field of solar origin threads that plasma, Ness explains. It generally keeps a direct connection back to the Sun. At Earth's distance the field averages only about six gamma, a whisper beside Earth's own field. Wind ions stream outward near four hundred kilometers per second on average, a few particles in every cubic centimeter.
nasa-tm-19700030148-flat-conductor-cable:
James R. Carden of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory wrote this report in October 1970. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It covers flat conductor cable built for limited rotary or straight-line motion, the kind of cable that must flex again and again inside moving equipment.

Carden reports the cable's mechanical properties first: tensile strength, bending torque, and flexing endurance. A stiffness comparison then sets the flat cable against ordinary round wire cables. Later sections apply the cable to straight-line motion, including a rolling loop arrangement for drawers. The figures throughout let a designer judge whether the flat form would survive the motion a job demands.
nasa-tm-19710007015-experimental-verific:
NASA issued this preprint on an experimental check of the theory of weak turbulence. It reads a sequence of diffuse plasma resonances that were observed in space. Plasma is the charged gas that fills much of the space around Earth, and its faint resonances carry clues to its hidden motions.

Two space probes, the Alouette 2 and ISIS-A satellites, recorded the resonances in orbit. The author explains them through waves and particles acting on each other in a weakly turbulent plasma. One part of that picture is a wave instability tied to electrons circling in a magnetic field. He then compares the observed center frequencies with the values the theory requires. The resonances that lasted longest, he notes, match the states most favorable to that instability.
nasa-tm-19720018359-transonic-transport-:
Louis J Williams of the Office of Aeronautics and Space Technology summarized this transport study in May 1972, as NASA TM X-62,156. Williams worked in the Advanced Concepts and Missions Division at Moffett Field. The study asked what faster cruise speeds would buy future airliners. Higher speed promises a market edge over rivals. It also raises each aircraft's productivity, since one jet makes more trips. The designs targeted service entry in 1980.

All the aircraft studied were transcontinental swept wing designs. None was allowed to boom the ground with sonic shock. Each carried two hundred passengers over a twenty seven hundred nautical mile range. No cargo was carried in the study designs. Results compare the speed gains against their costs. The summary runs to forty six pages.
nature-s-serial-story:
Edward Payson Roe called his book Nature's Serial Story, and his preface tells why. A tired brain worker once told him life had begun to drag and lose its zest. Roe answers that such weariness seldom hits a person who has fallen in love with nature.

Mr and Mrs Clifford in the story are not wholly made up, Roe says. An old man in the tale loved his garden and fruit trees past eighty years. An invalid found comfort in flowers that Roe says he did not stretch. The story aims to draw readers outdoors, where each spring brings a fresh chapter.
on-heroes-hero-worship-and-the-heroic-in: Thomas Carlyle's 1841 lectures on great men: Odin, Muhammad, Dante, Shakespeare, Cromwell, Napoleon. Arguing that history is shaped by heroes, Carlyle thunders through biography as moral epic. Overblown and magnificent, the book shaped Victorian ideas of greatness and coined the phrase "hero-worship."
once-aboard-the-lugger-the-history-of-ge:
Arthur Stuart-Menteth Hutchinson wrote this novel of George and Mary. The contents divide the tale into three books. Book one treats George, his melancholy, and a hospital. A heroine makes a magnificent arrival late in book one. Book two turns to Mary's memory and mind.

Book three mixes love and war in its chapters. Bridges, letters, and dinners at Palace Gardens appear. Hutchinson jokes that some chapters may be skipped. It calls the tale a salt-sprayed romance aboard a lugger. Tender humor and sea air fill the story.
ontario-teachers-manuals-history:
Ontario's Department of Education issued this history teaching manual. Copp Clark published it in Toronto, copyrighted in 1915. The minister of education authorized the book for teachers. It opens with the public and separate school course. Chapter one treats the aims and stages of study.

Chapter two gives general methods for teaching history. Chapter three treats correlation with other school subjects. Special topics include current events, local material, and civics. Chapter five gives illustrative lessons for each form. A devices section closes the practical guidance. The manual helped Ontario teachers plan history lessons well.
our-lady-saint-mary:
J. G. H. Barry's Our Lady Saint Mary, published in 1922 and dedicated to the League of the Blessed Virgin, is an Anglo-Catholic book of devotion to the Virgin Mary. An epigraph from Origen heads it: would that I might be called a fool by the unbelieving for believing such things. The contents follow Mary's whole story. The Annunciation and Visitation come first. Cana, Holy Week, and the Crucifixion follow. The Resurrection, the Ascension, and the descent of the Holy Spirit close her earthly story. The Assumption and the Coronation end the book.

Before the life comes doctrine: the book's first part takes up loyalty and the meaning of worship, opening with the Church's collect rejoicing in Mary's joys. Barry writes for believers who keep her feasts, and the life is told as a sequence of mysteries to be contemplated rather than argued.
parisians-in-the-country:
Honoré de Balzac wrote the two works bound together in Parisians in the Country. The first, The Illustrious Gaudissart, dates from 1832, near the height of his powers. The second, The Muse of the Department, came more than ten years later. An editor's introduction compares the two pieces and traces Gaudissart through Balzac's other novels.

Gaudissart is a travelling salesman, full of talk and confidence, whom country villagers manage to outwit. The Muse of the Department turns to provincial literary ambition and gives a long, careful portrait of the man of letters Lousteau. Together the pair show Balzac moving between Paris and the provinces, his two great territories.
peggy-from-kerry: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Peggy from Kerry, the title page, copyright page, and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Mrs. L. T. Meade and illustrator Martin Lewis, and Hurst and Company published the book in New York with copyright dated 1912. The frontispiece shows two girls, Molly and Jessie, stealing into a room to look at the sleeping Peggy.
pipe-and-pouch-the-smoker-s-own-book-of-:
Joseph Knight compiled Pipe and Pouch, subtitled The Smoker's Own Book of Poetry, in Boston in 1895. He dedicated the anthology to his friend and fellow-smoker Walter Montgomery Jackson. He gathered poems all turning on pipes, tobacco, and the pleasures of smoking.

Knight's preface admits this is an age of anthologies. He argues that broad collections have met with favor, since they serve both the busy man and the student of literature. Here the range is narrow on purpose: one subject, many poets. The volume offers smokers a shelf of verse matched to their habit. It is chosen for companionship rather than for study.
pipes-o-pan-at-zekesbury:
James Whitcomb Riley published Pipes O'Pan at Zekesbury in Indianapolis in 1895. He dedicated it to his brother John A. Riley, with memories of the old home. Riley was Indiana's beloved dialect poet, and Zekesbury is his invented Hoosier village.

The book opens with At Zekesbury and then a long run of Down Around the River poems. They include Romancin', Has She Forgotten, A' Old Played-Out Song, The Lost Path, Babyhood, The Days Gone By, and Mrs. Miller. Many titles are spelled in country dialect. The subjects are home, courtship, childhood, and loss. Readers who know Riley's homespun voice will find it here in a full village setting.
plays-acting-and-music-a-book-of-theory:
Arthur Symons wrote Plays, Acting and Music: A Book of Theory, published in London in 1909. Symons was a critic of drama, music, and dance. The book is dedicated to Maurice Maeterlinck, in friendship and admiration, as its front pages state.

Essays in the first part judge great stage figures of the day. Symons writes on Sarah Bernhardt, Coquelin in the plays of Molière, and Sir Henry Irving, among others. One essay takes up Nietzsche on tragedy, and the book opens with a piece called An Apology for Puppets. Later essays turn to drama itself, with pieces on Tolstoi and on trained and untrained actors.
podcast-dannyjones-nCbtQCikARY:
Bek Lover joins Danny Jones for a talk on God, aliens, and what he calls the demonic realm. Lover is a repeat guest who reads UFO lore through a strong Christian lens. His view ties craft in the sky to spirits in scripture.

Lover argues that so-called aliens are in truth fallen beings from the Bible. He links sightings, abduction tales, and end-times signs into one frame. Jones lets him preach the frame at length, then tests it. Listeners get a faith-first take on the UFO wave. The library files the talk as an archive record of the guest's beliefs.
podcast-joerogan-71XphFGuORY:
Religion professor Diana Walsh Pasulka joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2091. Pasulka wrote American Cosmic, a study of UFO belief drawn from fieldwork with scientists and experiencers. She approaches saucers the way scholars approach faith, which sets her apart from most guests on the topic.

She explains why smart people treat UFO events as sacred, and how tech leaders quietly fund the research. Rogan asks where her study left her own beliefs. The episode offers a rare angle on the phenomenon: not whether the craft are real, but why the stories around them carry such religious weight.
podcast-joerogan-sKwq7mpBTrY:
Congressman Tim Burchett of Tennessee talks UFOs with Joe Rogan in episode 2495 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Burchett is one of the loudest voices in Congress demanding that the government release what it knows. He brings a plain, funny, country style to a topic full of suits.

Burchett describes the pushback he says lawmakers get when they ask about secret programs. He talks about hearings, whistleblowers, and the money trail behind hidden projects. Rogan asks what Burchett himself believes is flying in our skies. The episode gives disclosure a rare insider who speaks like a neighbor, not a press release.
podcast-tuckercarlson-8zPJGAQYMRY:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton joins Tucker Carlson to talk border strain. Carlson calls immigration the state's most pressing problem. It has changed Texas in every way, he says.

Paxton expects new federal orders to bite fast, based on past terms. He recalls politics from the Bush years onward. The title charges that George Soros shields cartels from the law. It also notes Paxton's blacklist by Fox News. Paxton presents himself as a fighter punished for his stands. The episode gives Texas voters his case in full. The fight, he insists, is far from over.
poetic-sketches-a-collection-of-miscella:
Thomas Gent issued his Poetic Sketches in a second edition in 1808, dedicating the collection to George Canning, then Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. Gent praises Canning as no less distinguished for scholarship than for statesmanship, and signs himself a faithful and devoted servant. The epigraph begs mercy with a joke: spare me when I do my best to make as much waste paper as the rest.

Gent, a working writer who had known poverty in Ireland and England. Filled his sketches with occasional and miscellaneous verse, the poems of a man writing for patrons, newspapers, and survival. His humility was real; he never had the leisure or money to write for posterity alone. The dedication shows the machinery of Regency literature plainly, a tradesman-poet laying his book at a great minister's feet and hoping for protection in return.
poetry:
Arthur Quiller-Couch, the Cornish critic known as Q, opens his book on poetry with Plato's tale of Er, the soldier who died. Lay twelve days on the funeral pile, and returned to tell of the spindle of Necessity turning in heaven, with sirens singing one harmony on its whorls. Quiller-Couch draws his moral early: beneath all guesswork, mankind grasps one certainty, that the universe rests on ordered motion. That harmony is the fact every account of things must face.

From that cosmic image he turns to the sun, moon, and stars of the almanac, motions men predicted for centuries before gravitation named their law. The book argues that poetry belongs to this deep human pattern-making, older than science and still its kin. Readers meet a don who writes like a sailor: learned, plain, and determined to keep poetry a living part of ordinary education.
rebecca-mary:
Annie Hamilton Donnell built this book for young readers around a small girl named Rebecca Mary, in nine linked tales. Their titles include The Thousand Quilt, The Bible Dream, The Cookbook Diary, and The Feel Doll. Two tales, The Plummer Kind and Un-Plummered, suggest a family thread running through the set.

The first tale, The Hundred and Oneth, finds Rebecca Mary sewing and counting her stitches aloud. She nears the hundred and first stitch she has long awaited, and her face pales with the wait. She puts off the last stitch until Thomas Jefferson crows. Thomas Jefferson is a snow-white rooster hunting under the currant bushes nearby.
recollections-of-calcutta-for-over-half-:
Montague Massey wrote this account of Calcutta as he knew it for more than fifty years, printed there in 1918 with pictures. He issued it for the benefit of the Red Cross Fund. The book is dedicated to Lady Carmichael, founder of the Bengal Women's War Fund.

Massey warns readers at the start that his pages hold no startling secrets, and some tales must stay buried. Much of the book describes how the city changed since his arrival in the sixties. Streets and buildings, public and private, were rebuilt or added in those years. His friend Walter Exley of the Statesman staff urged him to write.
redgauntlet-a-tale-of-the-eighteenth-cen:
Sir Walter Scott framed this tale of the eighteenth century as thirteen letters, then twenty-three chapters, with notes and a glossary at the end. His introduction takes Jacobite feeling as his theme. The rising of 1745, he says, gave fiction a subject founded on real events, still remembered without much bitterness.

The Highlanders who formed the chief strength of Charles Edward's army draw Scott's praise as brave to romance. Their prince marched on foot at their head, bore fatigue, and beat regular forces in three battles. Scott likens his later course to a shooting star: brief, brilliant, then dark. That lost cause supplies the tale's ground.
rosemary-a-christmas-story: C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote Rosemary, a Christmas story first held under a 1906 copyright and issued in New York by A. L. Burt. The book has eight pictures by William Hatherell. Its front piece shows Evelyn and Rosemary climbing hand in hand while Hugh carries two huge baskets. The contents list seven chapters, among them The White Girl on the Terrace, Rosemary in Search of a Father, Fairy Fathers Must Vanish, and The White Figure at the Door.
roy-blakeley-his-story: Percy Keese Fitzhugh arranged Roy Blakeley, His Story, with pictures by Howard L. Hastings, issued in New York in 1920 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. The title page calls the book the true narrative of Roy's adventures, and those of his troop, on land and sea and in the mud, chiefly in the mud. The tale is taken from the Troop Book of the 1st Bridgeboro Troop and arranged by Roy himself, with help from Pee-wee Harris and Fitzhugh.
sanctuary:
Edith Wharton opens Sanctuary at Part I with Kate Orme yielding herself, for once, wholly to happiness. Youth, the narrator says, does not often let itself feel undividedly happy, since such a feeling comes from selection and setting aside, beyond the reach of a young, grasping hold on life. Kate's joy soaks through every faculty as a spring rain soaks into a sprouting meadow. Nothing within the last two months, since her engagement to Denis Peyton, has distinctly added to her happiness. No addition, she would have affirmed, could perceptibly raise a total already beyond counting.

Inwardly and outwardly, the conditions of Kate's life are unchanged, yet the air that once held flitting wings now seems to pause over her, and she can trust herself to their shelter. Many influences built the centre of brooding peace she finds.
simple-italian-cookery:
Antonia Isola gathered these Italian receipts under plain heads: soups, macaroni and other pastes, rice, sauces, eggs, fish, vegetables, meats, salads, and desserts. Beef soup stock leads the book, built from a pound of round beef, bones, carrots, potatoes, onion, and tomato in two quarts of water.

The stock simmers two hours over a slow fire, gains two spoonfuls of sherry, then strains through cloth. A turkey leg or chopped beef enriches it further. Isola writes for American kitchens, giving Italy's home cooking in clear measures and calm steps that new cooks can trust.
sowing-and-reaping-a-temperance-story:
Frances E. W. Harper wrote Sowing and Reaping, a temperance story, brought back here as a rediscovered novel in an edition by Frances Smith Foster. Chapter I opens on street talk: John Andrews has given up his saloon, and a fine business it was. One voice calls the move a foolish thing and guesses that his wife, who never seemed happy in the trade, was set hard against it.

A second voice owns that he prizes the peace of his home above all, and would not take up work that gave his wife constant pain. The first speaker scorns such rule by a wife: her place, he holds, is at home at her own affairs, while how he gets the living is his affair alone. The clash of views sets the tale's ground at once: drink sold for gain, weighed against the cost at home.
sowing-and-sewing-a-sexagesima-story: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote Sowing and Sewing, a Sexagesima story, printed at New York by E. P. Dutton and Co. Her short preface hopes that readers who spy hints of a sacred parable under the tale will not think the use of its lesson out of place. The contents open with The Sermon, then The Sunday School, and then The Working Party.
spanish-life-in-town-and-country: L. Higgin wrote Spanish Life in Town and Country for the set Our European Neighbours, edited by William Harbutt Dawson. The set also names French, German, Russian, Dutch, Swiss, Italian, Danish, and other lives. Chapters on Portuguese life in town and country, by Eugène E. Street, join Higgin's work in the same book. One picture shows a church scene, with the mantilla and veil on display.
stories-of-later-american-history:
Wilbur F. Gordy, once superintendent of schools at Springfield, Massachusetts, wrote Stories of Later American History for Charles Scribner's Sons, who copyrighted it in 1915. Gordy had already written several school histories, and this one carries maps and illustrations.

The contents open with Patrick Henry and Samuel Adams, the stirrers of revolt, then reach the war beginning near Boston and George Washington in the Revolution. The book tells the founding era through its leaders and turning points. That gives school readers a clear, story-shaped path into the nation's early years. Gordy used the same manner in his earlier volumes. Those covered explorers and colonial days.
stories-of-mystery: Only the front matter is present here. It holds a publisher's list of the eighteen Little Classics volumes. The list runs from Exile and Intellect through Comedy, Love, and Nature. A title page follows. It names this the eighth volume, Mystery, edited by Rossiter Johnson. Houghton Mifflin printed it at Boston and New York in 1914, under an 1875 copyright. No contents list or story text appears in these pages, so nothing about the tales inside can be told from them.
studies-in-forensic-psychiatry:
Bernard Glueck, an instructor in psychiatry and neurology at George Washington and Georgetown universities, wrote Studies in Forensic Psychiatry as Criminal Science Monograph No. 2, a supplement to the journal of the American Institute of Criminal Law and Criminology.

Glueck brings the doctor's eye to the courtroom's problems: how mental illness and defect show up in crime, prison life, and the offender's fitness to be tried or punished. The text leans on case work and on German and other foreign study, with terms like prison psychoses running through it. The monograph belongs to the early push to make psychiatry a working part of criminal law rather than an afterthought.
tales-of-terror-and-mystery:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's Tales of Terror and Mystery joins six tales of terror with six tales of mystery in one volume. The terror side lists The Horror of the Heights and The Leather Funnel, while the mystery side lists The Lost Special and The Man with the Watches.

The Horror of the Heights opens with a plea that the strange tale of Joyce-Armstrong is no hoax. Its narrator warns that our safe world may sit close to a strange new risk high above us. Readers get Doyle away from Sherlock Holmes, working with dread, odd facts, and crimes that test reason to its edge.
tangled-trails-a-western-detective-story: William MacLeod Raine wrote Tangled Trails, billed as a western detective story. Rights were held in 1921. A third printing is dated March 1922. Grosset and Dunlap of New York issued the book. Twenty-nine chapters are listed. Titles include No Altruist, Wild Rose Takes the Dust, and Foul Play. Later titles name The Coroner's Inquest and The Lady with the Violet Perfume. The Brass Bed and The Finger of Suspicion Points close the list.
ten-englishmen-of-the-nineteenth-century:
James Richard Joy wrote Ten Englishmen of the Nineteenth Century in 1902 to teach the age's history through lives rather than dry fact lists. Joy gave the book to his daughter Helen, and his preface lays out the plan in plain terms.

Joy says ten lives can show the main course of events more clearly than a crowded straight history could. With one exception, his men come from public life, in politics or war. George Stephenson stands as the lone exception, since his better locomotive changed travel and trade for the whole nation. Readers get a guided tour of a century through the men who led it, aimed at students.
the-advance-of-english-poetry-in-the-twe: William Lyon Phelps, Lampson Professor of English Literature at Yale, wrote The Advance of English Poetry in the Twentieth Century. Its thanks pages name the poets whose work is quoted, grouped by their publishing houses: Thomas Hardy, John Masefield, W. B. Yeats, Edgar Lee Masters, and Amy Lowell among the Macmillan names, and Walter De La Mare, Edward Thomas, Robert Frost, and Carl Sandburg among the Holt names.
the-advance-of-science-in-the-last-half-:
T. H. Huxley wrote The Advance of Science in the Last Half-Century, printed in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1889. Huxley was a fellow of the Royal Society and the age's best-known voice for science. His essay surveys fifty years of change.

Huxley calls the vast growth of factory output the most clear mark of the age. Machines, better methods, and fresh inventions drove it, with swift new means of travel and message close behind. He says these gains raised the shared standard of comfort, checked plague and famine, and shrank the blocks of time and space. Readers get a crisp, broad view of how steam, wire, and lab work remade daily life in one lifetime.
the-american-judiciary: Contents pages alone present The American Judiciary by Simeon E. Baldwin, styled LL.D., with no year shown. Part One treats the nature and reach of court power in the United States. It covers English roots and the split of judging from lawmaking and ruling. It also covers ties to the political branches and the force of past rulings. Last come the power to grow unwritten law and the power to void false law. Part Two turns to how American courts are set up and do their daily work.
the-anti-slavery-harp-a-collection-of-so:
William W. Brown, who names himself a fugitive slave on the title page, gathered The Anti-Slavery Harp at Boston in June 1848 as a cheap songbook for anti-slavery meetings. In his preface Brown says public demand for newer songs moved him to make the set. He thanks the makers of the Liberty Minstrel and the Anti-Slavery Melodies for some pieces.

Most of the songs, Brown notes, had never been published before, and some had never been in print at all. He offers the book to all true friends of the slave. The first song asks, to the air of Bride's Farewell, whether a man and brother ought not to be free, since Christ died for him as for others.
the-ashiel-mystery:
Mrs. Charles Bryce opens this detective story with Sir Arthur Byrne falling ill after three summers at a small consulate above the lonely Black Sea. A line from Robert Louis Stevenson heads the book, warning that the reader of a police romance always has far more wit than its writer.

Byrne takes sick leave and hurries home to scatter guineas in Harley Street, London's street of doctors. He feels the doubts of a strong man who has never known a headache and now finds all is not well. Outwardly he jokes that drains are to blame: once back to sound sewers, he tells fellow passengers on the boat to Constantinople, he will be himself again.
the-avalanche-a-mystery-story:
Gertrude Atherton called her 1919 book a mystery story and dedicated it to Charles Hanson Towne. Price Ruyler suspects that his wife Hélène hides a secret, perhaps one buried by the San Francisco earthquake and fire. Her quiet mother-in-law hints at a past of her own.

Ruyler recalls a happy first year and a half of marriage, then small changes in his wife's mood and habits. She had spent freely after leaving a strict girlhood in an old family villa at Rouen, France. He wonders what the grey cloud between them means. Suspense grows from manners and money, not from a crime shown at the start.
the-beginner-s-american-history:
D. H. Montgomery published a beginner's history in Boston in 1893 with Ginn and Company, after a copyright in 1892. A frontispiece shows the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor, a gift from the people of France. Montgomery also wrote a series called Leading Facts of History.

In a prefatory note he says the little book is not a shortened form of his larger history, but a new and distinct work. Its aim is to present, clearly and with care for sound sources, facts from the lives of chief founders and builders of America. Pupils beginning the study of history are its intended readers, aided by many illustrations.
the-belfry:
May Sinclair published her novel in 1916, naming herself as author of The Three Sisters. Book one is called My Book, and its narrator warns that the story cannot be published as it stands for another generation. The people in it, thank Heaven, are still alive.

He wonders how they managed their life at all, since they seem to have taken every risk. One of them had the luck the narrator feels should have been his own. Yet the telling of the story remains the narrator's alone. He admits he has already published its end, but only in altered form, and claims the big final matter as his to relate.
the-belles-of-canterbury:
Anna Bird Stewart wrote a one-act play for eleven girls in 1912, priced at twenty-five cents and published by Samuel French in New York and London. Stewart dedicated it to Dorothy Conrey. Its subtitle calls it a Chaucer tale out of school.

Four pupils, freshman through senior at a girls' school, form one group of persons. Figures from Chaucer's Canterbury Tales form the other: the Wife of Bath, the Prioress, and two nuns from the Prologue, and Emily from the Knight's Tale. School life and old poetry meet on stage, giving young players both modern roles and famous literary parts to speak.
the-bittermeads-mystery:
E. R. Punshon built a mystery from chapter headings that begin with a lone passenger. A fight in the woods, a coincidence, and a weeping woman follow. A discovery and a question-and-answer chapter lead to a heading joining captivity and capture.

An attic of mystery, a new gardener, and a problem deepen the puzzle. An avowal, invisible writing, and love-making at night are listed, then the sound of a shot. Later chapters name Robert Dunn's enemy, a visit to Wreste Abbey, and Ella's warning. Doubts and fears close the opening list, promising suspicion around a country house.
the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-country:
Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins in the Country, a tale in twenty-two parts. The parts start with a call to the country, the start, and the cat Snoop on the train. A long ride brings the twins to Meadow Brook. A picnic, fun in the woods, the Fourth of July, pea picking, a circus, a flood, and fresh-air camp fill the mid parts.

The first part opens on sweep day at the Bobbsey home. Freddie hears the bell and cries that the post man is at the door. Flossie says it is her turn to answer this week. Freddie spots a blue note case and cries that it is from Aunt Sarah. Both young folk race for the front door, and Freddie wins by a leap over a small couch in his path.
the-book-of-american-negro-poetry: James Weldon Johnson chose and edited The Book of American Negro Poetry, put out in New York by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1922. Johnson also wrote an essay for it on the Negro's gift for making new work. The list of poets starts with Paul Laurence Dunbar, whose songs here hold A Negro Love Song, Little Brown Baby, The Haunted Oak, and When de Co'n Pone's Hot. James Edwin Campbell and James D. Corrothers come next. Daniel Webster Davis and William H. A. Moore are also named.
the-book-of-the-epic-the-world-s-great-e: H. A. Guerber wrote The Book of the Epic: The World's Great Epics Told in Story, put out in 1913 with a first word by J. Berg Esenwein and sixteen plates from the great painters. Guerber had also written myths of Greece and Rome. The list starts with the Greek epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, then the Latin Aeneid. French epics come next, with The Song of Roland. The Spanish Cid, the Portuguese Lusiad, and the Italian Divine Comedy are also named.
the-brook-kerith-a-syrian-story:
George Moore wrote The Brook Kerith: A Syrian Story, dated 1916. It opens with a dedication to Mary Hunter. She had wished to give him a book for Christmas, could not tell what, and in her doubt gave him a Bible. That Bible, dated 1898 on the fly-leaf, lies on his table still. Moore says that Bible, itself a literature, led him into many others and into the society of scholars.

The story then starts with Joseph, a child on his grandmother's knee at the end of a summer evening. She tells him how Kish lost his asses and sent Saul to seek them. The servant shows a quarter of a shekel of silver to pay the seer. They walk into Arimathea and ask the maidens at the well if the seer has been in the city that day.
the-buccaneers-in-the-west-indies-in-the: C. H. Haring wrote The Buccaneers in the West Indies in the XVII Century, from Methuen in 1910. The book has ten maps and plates. Its first chapter is in two parts: the Spanish colonial system, and the freebooters of the sixteenth century. Then come The Beginnings of the Buccaneers and The Conquest of Jamaica. Tortuga, 1655-1664, and Porto Bello and Panama follow. The Government Suppresses the Buccaneers and The Buccaneers Turn Pirate close the main text. Appendices, a bibliography, and an index end the book.
the-builders-a-story-and-study-of-masonr: Joseph Fort Newton wrote The Builders: A Story and Study of Masonry, put out at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, by the Torch Press in 1915, with rights dated 1914. Newton's name bears the Litt. D. mark and his link to the Grand Lodge of Iowa. A verse from Kipling stands at the front, on a king and mason who cleared ground for a palace and found the wreck of a palace below the silt.
the-burglar-and-the-blizzard-a-christmas: Alice Duer Miller wrote The Burglar and the Blizzard: A Christmas Story, put out by Hearst's International Library Company in 1914, with art by Charlotte Harding. Miller had also written The Blue Arch. The list of plates tells more than the chapter heads do. One caption says it was a young lady who disposed of the silver. The tale opens with Geoffrey Holland standing in a restaurant, looking for the rest of his party, and no more of the page is shown.
the-bushman-life-in-a-new-country:
Edward Wilson Landor wrote The Bushman: Life in a New Country, a book on British colonial life with a plate of kangaroo hunting. His preface starts with the place of the colonies in the empire. The British colonies now form so prominent a portion of the empire, he says, that the public must grant some interest in their welfare. Too remote for sympathy and too powerless for respect, the colonies have rarely held a passing thought at home.

But the weakness of childhood passes, Landor says: the infant grows fast into strength, while the parent must own the growing usefulness of her offspring. In his remarks on colonial government, he warns, the system is assailed, not individuals. The proof, he says, is that the finest statesmen have all failed to distinguish themselves by good works while directing the colonies. Lord John Russell, Lord Stanley, and Mr. Gladstone are named.
the-cave-in-the-mountain-a-sequel-to-in-: Lieut. R. H. Jayne wrote this boys' adventure book, published in New York by the Mershon Company in 1894. It is billed as a sequel to In the Pecos Country, another of his tales. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing twenty-three chapters. Their titles speak of a strange guide, mining and countermining, fishing for a friend, and border chivalry.What the book holds past its front matter stays untold here.
the-champdoce-mystery:
Emile Gaboriau wrote this French detective novel, presented here as a sequel to Caught in the Net. Chapter I, headed A Ducal Monomaniac, opens on the road from Poitiers to London. The shortest route, readers learn, starts with the stage-coach to Saumur, booked for a prompt six o'clock start.

Gaboriau draws the small comedy of that start in close detail. The traveler rises early, hurries his toilet, and arrives flushed, only to find the hotel asleep and a drowsy waiter drifting about. Anger does no good, so the stranded group gathers at a small restaurant across the way for hot coffee. At length the conductor swears, the whip cracks, and the coach rolls. That slow, observed opening is classic Gaboriau groundwork for the crime tale to come.
the-channings-a-story: Mrs. Henry Wood, author of East Lynne and Johnny Ludlow, wrote this story, shown here in an edition dated 1901 and marked as the two hundred and tenth thousand. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here. Chapter titles name an inked surplice, bad news, Constance Channing, Roland Yorke, the cloister keys, and a mishap to the bishop.Past that front matter, the record is silent.
the-chosen-people-a-compendium-of-sacred:
A compendium of sacred and church history for school-children, by the author of The Heir of Redclyffe, is shown here in its fifth edition. Verses from Hebrews and from Lyra Innocentium stand at its head. The Lyra verses trace a change: once, heaven's light touched only one border of earth, but now each hour of the day brings its turn of sacrifice and praise.

The preface, cut short in what is present, begins by crediting friends who asked for the book. Its method rests on the writer's experience of what children need to be told. The aim is an intelligent grasp of the story, not a bare list of names and dates. Told in that spirit, the history runs from the prophets of old to the Son spoken of in the opening verse.
the-christian-a-story:
Hall Caine, author of The Manxman, wrote this story of faith and the outer world. A note before the tale sets its time scheme with care. The period is the last quarter of the nineteenth century, with no particular years intended. Three books take about six months each, then a half-year gap, then a fourth book of about six weeks.

Book I, The Outer World, opens on the morning of the 9th of May aboard the Isle of Man steamship Tynwald. She lies at the pier at Douglas, raising steam for Liverpool. Three people who matter to the tale stand among the passengers on deck. One is an old clergyman of seventy, with a sweet, mellow, childlike face. The second is a young clergyman of thirty. The third is a girl of twenty. Caine builds the novel on the crossing of those three lives.
the-chums-of-scranton-high-on-the-cinder: Donald Ferguson wrote this boys' school story, copyrighted in 1919 by the World Syndicate Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapters open with five nut foragers on the old quarry road. They move through training for a great tournament and a prowler caught in the act. A friendly ghost appears, and a great marathon race closes the list.Nothing inside the book follows its front matter.
the-counterpane-fairy:
Katharine Pyle wrote and drew the pictures for The Counterpane Fairy, published in New York by E. P. Dutton and Company with an 1898 copyright. Its contents list ten chapters, among them The Princess of the Golden Castle, The Magic Circus, At the Edge of the Polar Sea, The Ruby Ring, and Down the Rat-Hole.

Chapter I opens on Teddy, a small boy alone in bed at four in the afternoon while his worn-out mother rests. He is getting over a real illness, kept to milk and gruel, with a glass of milk by the bed and the cook Hannah singing below. He pages through Robinson Crusoe, looking at the bright pictures, then calls down to Hannah.
the-crest-wave-of-evolution-a-course-of-:
Kenneth Morris gave The Crest-Wave of Evolution as a course of lectures in history to the graduates' class in the Raja-Yoga College at Point Loma in the college year 1918-1919. The lectures were later serialized in Theosophical Path from March 1919 through July 1921. His contents sweep from Homer, the Greeks and Persians, and Socrates and Plato to the Mauryas of India, Confucius, Taoist tales, the beginnings of Rome, and Ireland.

In his opening lecture Morris says the course will not treat history as a record of wars and political changes, with little told of battles, murders, and sudden deaths. Instead the class will look for the cyclic movements beneath events and try to throw light on them.
the-custom-of-the-country:
Edith Wharton's The Custom of the Country, dated 1913, opens in the Hotel Stentorian. Undine Spragg snatches a note from her mother as a bell-boy brings it in, crying, Undine Spragg, how can you? The mother only smiles at her visitor and yields, as she always does.

The visitor is Mrs. Heeny, a stout, professional-looking woman in a waterproof with a shabby alligator bag at her feet. The Spraggs sit in heavy gilt armchairs in one of the hotel's Looey suites, its walls hung with salmon-pink damask and oval portraits of Marie Antoinette and the Princess de Lamballe. Mrs. Spragg wears a look of full detachment, like a wax figure in a show-window, her pale face soft and puffy. Mrs. Heeny praises Undine's lovely form with good-humored approval.
the-dangerous-age-letters-and-fragments-:
Karin Michaelis wrote The Dangerous Age in Danish; the English edition, printed in New York by the John Lane Company in 1911. It renders the work as letters and fragments from a woman's diary, and dedicates it to her brother-in-law, Baron Yoost Dahlerup. An introduction to the French edition by Marcel Prevost opens the volume.

Prevost calls it a strange book: a novel from the North with a solid build and a clear, bare form he terms purely Latin. It is a woman's novel of such full and violent sincerity that it matches famous confessions by men. Michaelis was unknown in France, he says, though German readers knew several of her novels. None stirred the curiosity, talk, and quarrels this one did; across Central Europe it was the most widely read novel of the moment, in edition after edition.
the-devil-s-dictionary:
Ambrose Bierce explains in an author's preface that The Devil's Dictionary began in a weekly paper in 1881 and ran at long gaps until 1906. That year much of it came out in covers as The Cynic's Word Book. The title was forced on him by the religious scruples of the last newspaper that carried the work. He had no power to reject it and no happiness in approving it.

By then a score of cynic books by imitators had flooded the country and dragged the word cynic so low that any book bearing it was discredited in advance. Bierce also notes that humorists had helped themselves to his definitions, many now current in popular speech. He claims his own again for readers who prefer dry wines to sweet and wit to humor. Opening entries start the alphabet: abasement is a decent mental attitude in the presence of wealth or power.
the-divine-comedy-volume-2-purgatory:
Volume two of Charles Eliot Norton's prose Divine Comedy holds Purgatory, and its contents list walks through all the cantos. Dawn of Easter on the shore, the angel's boat, and Cato open the climb. Then come the late-repentant, the valley of princes, the gate with seven marks cut on Dante's brow, and the ledges of pride.

Each canto gets a short prose summary before the text. The list alone maps the mountain: late prayers, carved scenes of humility, smoke for the wrathful, and dreams at dawn. Norton's clear notes make a hard poem easy to track.
the-divine-office-a-study-of-the-roman-b:
Rev. E. J. Quigley's study of the Roman Breviary, The Divine Office, is dated 1920. Its first part takes up broad questions: what the Breviary is, a short history of prayer in common, and how the Roman book stands next to others. Then it lists the parts of the church year, the calendar, and the rules that govern each day's office.

Later lists name each hour of prayer, from Matins and Lauds through Vespers and Compline, plus hymns, psalms, and canticles. The book serves priests and students who want the logic behind a daily round of prayer.
the-dore-lectures-being-sunday-addresses: The Dore Lectures on Mental Science, by Thomas Troward, is the work named at the front of this text. Only the old Project Gutenberg header pages are present here. They give the title and author, but no part of the lectures themselves. The record's title speaks of Sunday addresses at the Doré Gallery. The text's own title calls the work lectures on mental science. No more can be drawn from what is present.
the-duchess-of-wrexe-her-decline-and-dea:
Hugh Walpole's The Duchess of Wrexe, copyrighted in 1914, styles itself a romantic commentary on her decline and death. A note by Walpole heads the first book, The Rising City. He warns that this novel leads a group of three set in one place. Yet each book stands whole on its own. None is a mere sequel. Shared figures will recur, he adds.

An aged duchess rules a rising city by will and wealth. Her death loosens old chains on the young. Walpole writes of class and change with warmth and a keen eye.
the-early-bird-a-business-man-s-love-sto:
George Randolph Chester's The Early Bird, subtitled A Business Man's Love Story, was copyrighted in 1910 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company. Chester had won fame with The Making of Bobby Burnit, and Arthur William Brown drew the pictures. Contents name A Very Busy Young Man, Mr. Turner Plunges, and Greek Meets Greek.

Later chapters promise maraschino chocolates, a violent flirt, and matrimonial eligibility trials. A swift young deal-maker finds love slows his step. Chester writes of deals and hearts with the same brisk snap that made his name in magazines.
the-end-of-the-world-a-love-story:
Edward Eggleston's The End of the World, a love story printed in 1872 with thirty-two pictures, opens with a mock preface in the potential mood. Eggleston jokes that all book-writers agree prefaces are useless, yet write them with great pains, as if a book's fate hung on them. His trouble is choice: he has half a dozen fine prefaces in mind and may use but one.

Behind the jest stands a backwoods tale of a sect that sets a date for the world's end. Love and faith collide on the Ohio frontier. Eggleston wrote The Hoosier Schoolmaster.
the-english-church-in-the-eighteenth-cen:
Charles J. Abbey and John H. Overton wrote The English Church in the Eighteenth Century, here in a revised, shortened new edition from Longmans, dated 1896. Their note says the cut halved the book by dropping whole chapters and trimming quotes. Gone are the Jacobites, the essayists, church cries, and sacred poetry, which bore but loosely on church history.

What stands is still the same work, they hold: parsons, bishops, Methodists, and sleepy parishes in the age of Wesley and Whitefield. The book long served as the standard tale of a church too often mocked as asleep.
the-evil-genius-a-domestic-story:
Wilkie Collins's The Evil Genius, a domestic story set for his friend Holman Hunt, opens at a trial. Before the story starts, a jury scene frames Miss Westerfield's schooling. The jurymen retire to weigh their verdict. Their foreman leads them. He has the clearest head and readiest tongue of the twelve. Collins sorts them with dry wit: the hungry one, the sketching one, the fidgety one, the silent one who decides.

A governess, a broken marriage, and a stolen child drive the plot. Collins turns law and pity against each other. The tale keeps his gift for secrets in plain homes.
the-expansion-of-europe-the-culmination-:
Ramsay Muir's The Expansion of Europe, subtitled The Culmination of Modern History, sets a twofold aim in Muir's preface. World politics and imperial rivalry now shape every life, he says, yet most men lack a brief, clear survey of how that came to pass. His book gives one: broad at first, fuller as it nears his own day.

Muir taught modern history at Manchester. Second edition pages track sea empires from Portugal to the scramble for Africa. The book helped frame how a generation of students saw empire: as the main thread of modern times.
the-extraordinary-adventures-of-poor-lit:
A small children's tale from 1850, credited only to the author of Nothing At All, tells of little Henry, shut up in an old abbey for three weeks. The title page calls the story one founded on fact.

Henry, aged three, loses his mother on the lawn and cries for her. A rough village boy, Bill Boldface, scares him with a tale of a bloody pig in the wood that will eat her. The child runs to save her, falls, gets up, and meets his dog Fidelle. Fear, love, and a small child's brave rush carry the opening.
the-film-mystery: Arthur B. Reeve wrote The Film Mystery as a Craig Kennedy tale of science used in crime work. It is one of his famed detective books. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name a camera crime and a tiny scratch. They name a fatal script and an antivenin. They name poisons such as botulin toxin and physostigmin. A film fire and a phosphorus bomb close the list. All this shows a mystery built around a movie studio death and lab tests.
the-forest-of-vazon-a-guernsey-legend-of:
The Forest of Vazon is a Guernsey legend of the eighth century, printed at London in 1889, built on the tale of a forest drowned by the sea. Its preface owns that no true record of the island's early days stands.

The writer says that before its joining to Normandy in the tenth century, Guernsey's past rests on monkish tales, stone relics, and bits of Celtic work. Scholars date the great flood to March 709, when the sea swept away weak banks and took low forest land. Rocquaine Bay, Lihou, and the Hanois rocks mark the loss. Legend fills the gap that records leave.
the-four-faces-a-mystery: William Le Queux wrote The Four Faces as a mystery, and only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapter heads name the Angel Faces, a Hampstead mystery, a house in Grafton Street, a confession, a baron, dusky fowl, a Channel mystery, and faces unmasked at the end. Le Queux's past books named on the title page include The Death Doctor and Lying Lips. No chapter text can be read in what is present, so the plot cannot be told from these opening pages alone.
the-french-revolution-a-history:
Thomas Carlyle wrote The French Revolution as a history in three volumes, and this copy opens with the first, The Bastille. Book heads run from the death of Louis XV to the march of the Third Estate.

Carlyle starts in a paper age of petitions, windbags, and printed sheets. Calonne and Lomenie fail to fix the king's debts, the Parlement fights the court, and the States-General is called. The Third Estate grows electric, takes arms, and moves on the Bastille. Carlyle tells the tale in a wild, burning style, half sermon and half epic, that made the French revolt live for English readers as no plain chronicle had.
the-french-revolution-a-short-history:
R. M. Johnston, a Harvard history teacher, wrote The French Revolution as a short history, printed at New York in 1910. A front picture shows Voltaire, Marie Antoinette on her way to death, and Danton before the court.

Johnston gives the book to Rayner Neate in memory of old Pembroke days at Cambridge. Where Carlyle storms, a short history must sort: causes, the fall of the old rule, the rise of the assembly, war, the Terror, and the close. Johnston writes for students and general readers who need the whole vast tale in one brief, clear line of fact.
the-giant-hands-or-the-reward-of-industr:
Alfred Crowquill wrote The Giant Hands, a fairy tale printed at London in 1856 as one of his tales for the young. The words are split by syllables, in the manner of early reading books.

Poor little Willie comes home from the forest bent under a load of wood, hungry and worn. His father died in the spring, and his mother toils for a scant living. No pot stands on the fire for their dinner. Willie vows this must not go on: he is growing big and strong, with hands that ought not to be idle. Work, in the tale's plain moral, brings its own strange reward.
the-golf-course-mystery:
Chester K. Steele wrote The Golf Course Mystery. A contents list has twenty-four chapters. They run from Putting Out and The Nineteenth Hole to Morocco Kate, Ally. They name an inquest, poison plants, and a private safe. Chapter I, Putting Out, opens on a clear, calm day. Blue sky and flooding sunshine fill it.

Nothing in that fine day hinted at the tragedy so close at hand. The tragedy puzzled the authorities. It nearly wrecked the happiness of several innocent people. An osprey hangs over the inlet. It peers into the water with eager, far-seeing eyes. Then it folds its wings and darts down. The calm scene and the bird's strike set up a death on the golf course. They set up the hunt for its cause.
the-gracchi-marius-and-sulla-epochs-of-a:
A. H. Beesley wrote The Gracchi, Marius and Sulla. It is a volume in the Epochs of Ancient History series. It is dated 1921, with maps. What is present here is a set of full chapter summaries. They trace Tiberius Gracchus and his land proposals. They trace the grievances of the holders, his clash with Octavius, and his murder.

The summaries go on to Caius Gracchus. They cover his corn law, his jury law, and his law on the taxation of Asia. They cover his colonies and his bid to give the franchise to the Italians. Drusus outbids him, and he is rejected for a fresh term. He too is murdered, though some of his laws stay in force. A further summary opens the Jugurthine War. It names the legacy of Attalus and Jugurtha's intrigues at Rome. The book gives late Roman republic history in tight, fact-packed form.
the-gray-goose-s-story:
Amy Prentice wrote The Gray Goose's Story. It is one of Aunt Amy's Animal Stories. It has thirty-two illustrations and a frontispiece in colors by J. Watson Davis. The tale opens by the pond beyond the apple orchard. Aunt Amy loves to wander there on pleasant afternoons. She meets her bird and animal friends there. All of them are ready to tell her stories.

There she sees Mr. Frisky Squirrel and old Mr. Plodding Turtle. She sees Mr. Bunny Rabbit too. Only yesterday, she says, did she meet the gray goose. That was owing to Master Teddy's mischief. Walking in search of a storyteller, she heard an angry hissing. She feared a snake. Instead she found two geese, scolding in their own fashion. One was the gray goose, who soon became her friend. That goose is the teller of this tale for young readers.
the-green-mirror-a-quiet-story:
Hugh Walpole wrote The Green Mirror, a quiet story. George H. Doran Company published it in New York in 1917. The book is dedicated to Dorothy, who first introduced the author to Katherine. A letter to Dorothy stands at the front. In it Walpole tells the book's history. He finished it in August 1914. He did not look at it again until the autumn of 1915. Then he revised it while getting well after an illness.

The world, he says, is now very different from the world of the story. The book may seem slow in development and uneventful in movement. It belongs to a day that already feels old-fashioned. Yet he has too warm an affection for Katherine, Philip, Henry, and Millicent to destroy their signs. The love of England, he says, is the text of the book.
the-hampstead-mystery:
John R. Watson and Arthur J. Rees wrote The Hampstead Mystery, dated 1916. Chapter one opens with a phone call between Detective-Inspector Chippenfield of Scotland Yard and Inspector Seldon at Hampstead. Chippenfield has received a rough, printed note on a cheap sheet of paper, and its spelling is broken up to hide who wrote it.

The note claims that Sir Horace Fewbanks was murdered in the night, shot through the heart, and that his body lies in the library at Riversbrook. Seldon reacts with shock at the news that a judge has been killed. The call sets a police inquiry in motion, with an unknown writer at the center of the puzzle.
the-history-of-richard-raynal-solitary: Robert Hugh Benson wrote The History of Richard Raynal, Solitary. A Latin dedication stands at the front. It is addressed in part to one who does not know. The contents list sections in an old style. One tells how Master Richard cried out in Westminster Hall. Another tells of his speaking with the King's Grace. A later section is called Of the Dark Night of the Soul. The list ends with How Master Richard Went to God. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-history-of-rome-book-v-the-establish: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome, Book V, on the establishment of the military monarchy, translated with the author's sanction by William Purdie Dickson, D.D., LL.D., professor of divinity in the University of Glasgow. The German original is named as Roemische Geschichte, Fuenftes Buch. The edition is called a new edition, revised throughout with recent additions. Only the title page and a preparer's note on marking foreign words in plain text are present here.
the-hunt-ball-mystery: Sir William Magnay wrote this detective novel, published in 1918. His earlier books include A Prince of Lovers. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The chapter headings outline the case. An intruder comes first. Stained flowers and a streak on a cuff follow. A missing guest and a locked room appear. The mystery of Clement Henshaw takes over, and Gervase Henshaw doubts. Later chapters send Gifford into the wood. A lost brooch and a churchyard end the list.
the-infant-s-delight-poetry:
Small children were the audience for these verses. The words are broken into syllables throughout. Beginners could sound them out that way. The first poem praises blind man's buff. Children play it beside the winter fire. No game sets them laughing and glowing like it. The Dead Robin tells a short, sad story. Minnie feeds sparrows and robins each winter morning. They come to her window for crumbs and grain.

One robin was bolder than the rest. It perched on her finger and won her best care. One sad morning it did not hop at its name. She found it dead on the ground. A third piece turns to scripture. All Things Obey God quotes the command given to the snow. The mix is typical of Victorian nursery books. A game, a pet's death, and a hymn stand side by side.
the-jesus-of-history: A study of the historical Jesus is framed here by two datelines. Poona, August 1916, signs one page. A foreword from Lambeth is signed Randall Cantuar. Its date is Advent Sunday, 1916. Only the contents are present here. The chapters themselves do not appear. The plan opens with the gospels as sources. Canons for studying a figure follow. A caution against mere antiquarian interest comes next. Childhood and youth are rebuilt partly from the parables. The man and his mind close the list shown.
the-jute-industry: T. Woodhouse and P. Kilgour wrote this volume on the jute industry. It runs from seed to finished cloth. Pitman's Common Commodities and Industries series issued it. Woodhouse headed weaving and designing at Dundee Technical College. The opening pages here give way to advertisements. Dundee machinery firms fill them. Bridge, Parker, and Fairbairn Lawson Combe Barbour appear. Hall, Craig, and Urquhart Lindsay follow. Only those advertisements and the title matter are present here. The industry's chapters themselves do not appear.
the-land-of-mystery:
Edward S. Ellis wrote adventure fiction for young readers, and his tale first carried an 1889 copyright before a 1901 Street and Smith issue. Chapter one places four white men and three Native guides in a canoe on the upper Xingu River. They have traveled a thousand miles from the Amazon toward the Matto Grosso table land in Brazil.

The party trades beads and bright goods for local articles along the banks. Fruit hangs within reach, and riverside peoples watch the strangers with awe. Ellis builds a remote river world where each new bend promises unknown peoples and danger.
the-laurel-bush-an-old-fashioned-love-st:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, author of John Halifax, Gentleman, opens her old fashioned love story with a very ugly bush. The lopsided laurel stands by a garden gate, hollow trunk and heavy branch shaped by years of growth. Its owners use a fork in the branches as a rough letter box.

Wild boys staying with their grandmother find a sparrow nest inside that box. Their governess Fortune Williams bears the cruel nickname Misfortune from the boys. A young tutor named Robert Roy, hired from St Andrews to keep order, has already scolded them for the name.
the-law-of-the-land-of-miss-lady-whom-it: Emerson Hough published his Southern novel in 1904, with illustrations by Arthur I. Keller. Only the title page and the contents of book one are present here, naming Miss Lady, a visitor, a question of valuation, a drum, a bell, and a volcano among its chapters. John Eddring, billed as a gentleman of the South who reads a deeper meaning in the law, does not yet appear. The mystery plot itself does not appear in this record.
the-leading-facts-of-english-history: D. H. Montgomery wrote his school history for the Leading Facts of History series, in a revised edition carrying copyrights through 1912. Only the title pages, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here, listing periods from Britain before written history through Roman Britain, the Saxons and Normans, and the Plantagenets. Montgomery motto from Stubbs says the past lives for anyone learning how the present came to be. The history chapters themselves do not appear in this record.
the-library:
Andrew Lang wrote about books and book collecting for Macmillan in London in 1881, with a chapter on modern English illustrated books by Austin Dobson. His prefatory note shares credit widely. Pages on illuminated manuscripts and early printed books came from the Reverend W. J. Loftie.

Lang also reprints pages on the biblioklept, a book thief figure, from the Saturday Review. Proof help came from a Bodleian sub librarian. Readers get essays on manuscripts, rare books, bindings, and collectors habits, written for lovers of libraries rather than for scholars alone. Each essay treats books as companions, not trophies.
the-life-of-william-carey-shoemaker-miss:
George Smith wrote his life of William Carey, the shoemaker who became a Baptist missionary in India. His preface sorts out earlier attempts. Joshua Marshman promised a life on Carey death in 1834 yet died too soon, and Eustace Carey 1836 volume cut letters and journals badly.

Carey own test for any life survives in that preface. He told his nephew that credit for being a plodder would describe him justly, since plodding perseverance won everything he gained. John Marshman 1859 history of the Serampore mission adds a fuller record for Smith to use.
the-lilac-sunbonnet-a-love-story: S. R. Crockett, author of The Stickit Minister and The Raiders, wrote his Scottish love story around a lilac sunbonnet. Only the title page and contents are present here. A prologue by the wayside opens a list of thirty-six chapters. Blanket washing, a treasure trove, a cavalier Puritan, and a lesson in botany come early in that list. Later titles promise the Cuif before the session and a gipsy named Jess. The Galloway tale itself is missing from this record.
the-little-city-of-hope-a-christmas-stor:
F. Marion Crawford wrote The Little City of Hope, a Christmas story published by Macmillan in London in 1907. Its nine chapters all begin with the word "How," following John Henry Overholt, a man and a boy who found an imaginary city together. The opening chapter shows Overholt leaving the office of Mr. Burnside, who has just flatly refused his request.

Burnside remarks that hope is very cheap, and Overholt answers that this is fortunate for poor men. Later chapter titles promise bricks made without straw, a famine in the city, a siege, and a small boy doing a big thing. The result is a gentle tale about holding on to hope when money and luck run short.
the-loudwater-mystery:
Edgar Jepson's The Loudwater Mystery, dated 1920, opens at a country-house breakfast going badly. Lord Loudwater ignores his food and his wife, tugging his red-brown beard over a leader in The Times and making noises of disgust. When the cat Melchisidec, excited by grilled sole, rises against his trousers, it pricks his thigh with gentle claws. The lord springs up howling. He kicks at empty air and swears violently at his wife and the cat. Lady Loudwater leaves with the cat and finishes breakfast alone.

Considering her husband afterward, she reaches her usual conclusion: she owes him nothing whatever, and she detests him. The butler, too, scowls at his master's back. Jepson loads the opening with hatred inside a great house, the right weather for a mystery.
the-love-of-books-the-philobiblon-of-ric:
The Love of Books presents the Philobiblon of Richard de Bury in E. C. Thomas's English translation. A preface sketches the author. Richard de Bury (1281–1345), born near Bury St. Edmunds and educated at Oxford, tutored Prince Edward of Windsor, the future Edward III. On his pupil's accession he climbed through church and state offices, served twice as ambassador to Pope John XXII, and met Petrarch at Avignon, probably in 1330.

At the end of 1333 he became Bishop of Durham, enthroned before the King and Queen, the King of Scots, and the magnates north of the Trent. He later served as High Chancellor of England in 1334 and Treasurer in 1336. The preface frames the Philobiblon, a famous medieval praise of books, through the career of the courtier-bishop who wrote it.
the-loves-of-krishna-in-indian-painting-: W. G. Archer wrote The Loves of Krishna in Indian Painting and Poetry, with a frontispiece showing Radha and Krishna in a grove, a Kangra painting from the Punjab Hills dated 1785. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the chapters do not appear. The contents move through the Mahabharata, where Krishna is the hero, and the Bhagavata Purana. They follow him as cowherd and prince. They turn to the Krishna of poetry, including the Gita Govinda, and the Krishna of painting, with plates and commentary last.
the-mahatma-and-the-hare-a-dream-story:
H. Rider Haggard's The Mahatma and the Hare, a dream story, begins with two clippings from local papers of January and February 1911. Both report hares dying under the hunt. One swam out to sea under pressure from hounds and drowned as a boat reached her. Another stuck fast in the ice of a horse-pond and sank while the huntsman waded in after her. Haggard says the first extract must have impressed him. That night, or the next morning, the title and outlines of the fantasy came to him, including the command with which it ends.

He saw with particular clearness the Great White Road and a little hare traveling it toward the awful Gates. The contents promise the Mahatma, the Great White Road, and the hare's own account of shooting, coursing, and hunting.
the-making-of-mary:
Jean Forsyth's The Making of Mary was published in New York by the Cassell Publishing Company in 1895, in a series called The "Unknown" Library. Its prologue opens on a deserted farmhouse in western Michigan, rattled by a sturdy northeast wind. The building was never painted or repaired. Its windows stare like lidless eyes, and plenty of shingles are off the roof. Rain-drops follow one another through the rafters to the floor below. The house was only recently vacated, since a slab still smolders on the hearth of the wide kitchen fireplace.

Something almost human lies much too near it, wrapped in a ragged bedquilt. A gust down the chimney draws a faint cough from the bundle, then a sneeze bursts the quilt open to disclose an ill-clad little girl of six or seven. Forsyth starts with abandonment and a child alone.
the-malady-of-the-century:
Max Nordau's The Malady of the Century opens in a German inn, where chapter one, Mountain and Forest, finds five or six students drinking clear Affenthaler wine. Their caps with colored bands, facial scars, and swaggering manner mark them easily. The company rises noisily, overturning the wooden bench, while someone jokes about the defection of their melancholy friend Eynhardt, combining obstinacy with wisdom like Balaam's ass.

The contents map a philosophical novel in fourteen chapters: Vanity of Vanities, Heroes, A Lay Sermon, An Idyll, Symposium, Dark Days, A Seaside Romance, Tannhauser's Plight, and Consummation among them. Nordau, better known for social criticism, begins his fiction with student fellowship and drink before turning to the sickness his title names.
the-man-shakespeare-and-his-tragic-life-: Frank Harris wrote The Man Shakespeare and His Tragic Life Story, dedicating it to Ernest Beckett, later Lord Grimthorpe. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present, so the argument does not appear. The contents reveal his method: book one, Shakespeare Painted by Himself, reads the plays as self-portraiture. Chapters pair Hamlet with Romeo and Jaques. Others treat Macbeth, Falstaff, and Shakespeare's men of action. Book two turns to Shakespeare's love-story in the sonnets, then revenge, jealousy, lust, madness in Lear, and despair in Timon of Athens.
the-man-who-laughs-a-romance-of-english-: Victor Hugo subtitled The Man Who Laughs a romance of English history. Only the title page and part of the contents are present, so the novel itself does not appear. The contents open with two preliminary chapters, Ursus and The Comprachicos. Part one's first book, Night Not So Black as Man, brings chapters at Portland Bill and a child left alone.
